citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

derivations.claim: **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2).

**The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$.

**The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below.

**The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$.

**Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4).

**The trace property of $\varepsilon$.** We claim $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$ and simple $s$, which by linearity reduces to $z=H_w$: if $\ell(ws)>\ell(w)$ then $H_wH_s=H_{ws}$ has $\varepsilon$-value $\delta_{e,ws}=0$ as $ws\ne e$, while $H_sH_w$ is $H_{sw}$ or $H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ with $\varepsilon$-value $\delta_{e,sw}=0$ or $\delta_{e,sw}+(v^{-1}-v)\delta_{e,w}=0$; if $\ell(ws)<\ell(w)$ then $w\ne e$, $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, and both sides equal $\delta_{e,ws}+(v^{-1}-v)\delta_{e,w}=0$; for $w=e$ both sides equal $\varepsilon(H_s)=0$. Hence $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sH_w)$ for every $w$.

**$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$.

**Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x
e y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x
e y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x
e y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$.

**The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice.

boundaries.reason: The statement attaches the trace to the explicit A-basis of the finite Hecke algebra and every summation it uses runs over the nonempty interval u <= x in Bruhat order; there is no empty family to interpret.

boundaries.evidence: The zero element and zero scalar are in scope: step 1.1 proves A-bilinearity of the form so (0,h) and (h,0) vanish, and the membership (H_x,H_y) in vZ[v] asserted by step 8.2 includes the zero polynomial for x not equal y.

The rank-one situation is the base computation of the induction: step 2.1 starts at the length-zero endpoint with H_e the unit, and step 7.1 shows the matrix of the form in the normalized standard basis is the identity, which is the whole content when there is a single generator index.

No reducedness or genericity hypothesis is used: steps 4.1 and 5.1 treat the two possible directions of the length change, and the coefficient v^{-1}-v is kept symbolic throughout, so the specializations where that coefficient vanishes satisfy the same formal identities.

The length induction has the lower endpoint length zero, discharged as the base case inside step 2.1, and the ascent and descent cases of steps 4.1 and 5.1 exhaust the two sides of the strict inequality, which is the only endpoint dichotomy in the argument.

Choice-free: the trace is prescribed on the explicit basis {H_w} of a finite group in step 1.1, and the induction of step 2.1 ranges over the finite set of permutations; no selection from an infinite family is made.

boundaries.reason: Clauses (1) through (6) are separate well-definedness, bilinearity, adjunction and value assertions; the item asserts no biconditional, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse obligation arises: the statement does not compare two equivalent conditions, it lists six independent properties of the trace and of the form.

citations.quote:
**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric $S$-bilinear form on a graded bimodule that is invariant under both
actions in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.

Let $n\ge2$, let $D$ be the type-A diagrammatic Soergel category over
$k=\mathbb Q$ and let $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ be its Karoubi envelope
([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]). Then
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ is a Krull–Schmidt category, and for every
$w\in S_n$ there is an indecomposable object $D_w$ of $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$,
unique up to isomorphism, characterised as follows: $D_w$ is a direct summand of
the Bott–Samelson object of any reduced word for $w$, and is not isomorphic to a
shift of a summand of the Bott–Samelson object of a reduced word for any
$v<w$; it does not depend on the chosen reduced word, and every indecomposable
object of $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ is isomorphic to $D_w(d)$ for a unique pair
$(w,d)\in S_n\times\mathbb Z$. In particular the passage to isomorphism classes
of indecomposables up to shift is a bijection
$$S_n\longrightarrow\{\text{indecomposables of }\operatorname{Kar}(D)\text{ up to isomorphism and shift}\},\qquad w\mapsto D_w.$$

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $D=D_n$ be the type-A diagrammatic Soergel
category over $\mathbb Q$ with Karoubi envelope $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$
([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]), and let
$\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be the type-A Soergel category of
[[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]. Let
$\mathcal F:D\to\mathrm{BSBim}^{\bullet}$ be the graded monoidal word functor of
[[lem-the-type-a-diagrammatic-relations-hold-for-soergel-bimodules]] and let
$\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F):\operatorname{Kar}(D)\to\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be its
extension after adjoining finite sums and shifts, restricting to degree-zero
maps, and taking idempotent completions. Then:

1. $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$ is faithful and full: for all words
   $\underline x,\underline y$ the map
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_D(\underline x,\underline y)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(B_{\underline x},B_{\underline y}),\qquad g\longmapsto\mathcal F(g),$$ is an isomorphism of graded left $R$-modules,
   and the restriction of $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$ to every hom space of
   $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ is a bijection;
2. $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$ is essentially surjective: every object of
   $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ is isomorphic to the image of an object of
   $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ under $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$;
3. $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$ is a graded monoidal functor, so that
   $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal F)$ is an equivalence of graded monoidal
   categories.

For $n\le1$ both categories are generated under finite sums, shifts and summands by $R$ up to the fixed
identification and $\mathcal F$ is that identification, so the conclusion holds
there as well.

Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]],
[[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) and let $H_{S_n}$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$ with $q=v^{-2}$ and normalized generators
$H_i=v(T_i+1)$
([[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]). Then there is an
isomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
$$\Phi:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad \Phi([B_i])=H_i=v(T_i+1)\quad(1\le i\le n-1),\qquad \Phi(vX)=v\,\Phi(X),$$
equivalently $\Phi^{-1}(T_i)=v^{-1}[B_i]-1$ for every simple reflection. In
particular the classes satisfy
$$[B_i]^2=(v+v^{-1})[B_i]\qquad\text{in }K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
in agreement with the quadratic relation $H_i^2=(v+v^{-1})H_i$ of the Hecke
algebra, and $\Phi$ is the unique algebra isomorphism with $\Phi([B_i])=H_i$
and $\Phi(v)=v$, because the classes of the $B_i$ together with $v^{\pm1}$
generate $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ as a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

1. $h_\Delta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and
   semilinear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ of the coefficients:
   $h_\nabla(vX)=v^{-1}h_\nabla(X)$ and $h_\nabla([B_i])=H_i$; equivalently
   $h_\nabla=d\circ h_\Delta$, where $d$ is the semilinear algebra involution
   of $H_{S_n}$ determined by $d(v)=v^{-1}$ and $d(T_i)=T_i^{-1}$;
3. for every Bott–Samelson word $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ one has
   $h_\Delta(B_{\underline i})=h_\nabla(B_{\underline i})=H_{i_1}\cdots H_{i_r}$,
   and for every bimodule $M$ in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$ and simple reflection
   $s_i$ the simple-generator recursion
   $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$,
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$ holds; in the Elias–Williamson
   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

derivations.claim: **Base change of Hom and reduction.** For rational finite right-free graded bimodules $M,N$ and every degree $j$, the space $\operatorname{Hom}^j(M,N)$ is the kernel of the finitely many $\mathbb Q$-linear equations expressing left $R$-linearity, right $R$-linearity and degree-$j$ homogeneity on the finitely many coordinates of $M$; tensor product with the flat ring $\mathbb R$ preserves these kernels, so $\operatorname{Hom}^j(M^R,N^R)=\operatorname{Hom}^j(M,N)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, and this identification is compatible with composition, with shifts and with finite direct sums. Moreover $\overline{M^R}=\overline M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, because the right augmentation ideal of $S$ is the $\mathbb R$-span of the rational one and tensoring the right presentation $M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ with $S/S_+=\mathbb R$ gives $(\overline M)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$; also $\Delta_x(d)^R\cong R_x(d)$ for the graph bimodules, since these are free of rank one.

**Support cuts and top layers.** The support submodules $\Gamma_x$, $\Gamma_{\le x}$, $\Gamma_{\ge x}$ of [F3] are defined by kernels and images of multiplication by invariant elements and hence are compatible with scalar extension in the sense $\Gamma_x(M^R)=(\Gamma_xM)^R$; the top support layer of an indecomposable $B_w$ is, after extension, the single graph layer $\Delta_w$.

**Local endomorphism algebra over $\mathbb Q$.** The graded Hom space $\operatorname{End}(B_w)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$ in each degree by [F7], hence $A_w=\operatorname{End}^0(B_w)$ is a finite-dimensional unital $\mathbb Q$-algebra; since $B_w$ is indecomposable in the idempotent-complete category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, every idempotent of $A_w$ is $0$ or $1$, so $A_w$ is local. Restricting $\mathbb Q$-linear endomorphisms of $B_w$ to the top support layer $\Delta_w$ (a rank-one free module over the field $\mathbb Q$) gives a unital algebra homomorphism $A_w\to\operatorname{End}^0(\Delta_w)=\mathbb Q$ that is surjective, because scalars act as scalars on the layer; its kernel is therefore the unique maximal ideal $J_w$ of $A_w$, so $A_w/J_w=\mathbb Q$.

**Real endomorphism algebras and indecomposability.** By [F1] applied to the graded endomorphism space, $\operatorname{End}^0(B_w^R)=\operatorname{End}^0(B_w)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R=A_w\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, and this algebra is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb R$; since $J_w$ is nilpotent (a proper two-sided ideal of the finite-dimensional local algebra $A_w$), so is $J_w\otimes\mathbb R$, and every element of $A_w\otimes\mathbb R$ outside $J_w\otimes\mathbb R$ is invertible by a finite geometric series after lifting its nonzero residue class; hence $A_w\otimes\mathbb R$ is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. A nonzero idempotent endomorphism of $B_w^R$ would be $0$ or $1$ in the local algebra $\operatorname{End}^0(B_w^R)$, so $B_w^R$ is indecomposable.

**Labels and shifts over $\mathbb R$.** Every object of $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is a direct summand of a finite sum of shifts of real Bott-Samelson products, and each real Bott-Samelson product is the scalar extension of the corresponding rational product by [F1] and the monoidality of scalar extension; decomposing the rational object by [F2] and extending the finite decomposition gives that every real object is a summand of a finite sum $\bigoplus B_w^R(d)$. Since each direct summand has local endomorphism algebra by step 3.1, the Krull-Schmidt theorem in this idempotent-complete additive category gives that the object is a finite direct sum of copies of the $B_w^R(d)$, uniquely up to permutation, so real extension preserves labels and shifts; in particular every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$.

**Degree-zero endomorphisms under $S(w)$.** Assume $S(w)$, so $h_\Delta(B_w)=\underline H_w$ and $h_\nabla(B_w)=d(\underline H_w)=\underline H_w$ by [F4] and the bar-invariance of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis; by [F7] and [F5] the graded rank of $\operatorname{End}(B_w^R)$ is $\langle\underline H_w,\underline H_w\rangle=\sum_{u\le w}p_{u,w}^2$, a polynomial in $v$ with constant term $1$ by [F6] since $p_{u,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<w$. Hence $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{End}^0(B_w^R)=1$, and since the unital algebra $\operatorname{End}^0(B_w^R)$ contains the scalars $\mathbb R$ as a subfield and is one-dimensional over $\mathbb R$, it equals $\mathbb R$; no statement is made about the full graded endomorphism module, whose graded rank is the displayed polynomial, generally not $1$.

**Characters and reduction under scalar extension (3).** Let $M$ be rational with a $\Delta$-flag in the sense of [F3]; each layer $\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d)$ has $R$-rank one, hence the same multiplicity function over $\mathbb Q$ and over $\mathbb R$, and by step 1.1 and step 1.2 the extension of the flag is a flag of $M^R$ with the same shifts, so $(M^R:\Delta_x(d))=(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $h_\Delta(M^R)=h_\Delta(M)$, $h_\nabla(M^R)=h_\nabla(M)$; additivity on direct sums from [F3] gives the same for every $\mathbb Q$-defined object, and step 1.1 gives the reduction identity and the Hom identity. If two character identities hold after scalar extension, their coefficients lie in $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and scalar extension of the free $A$-module $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ is injective, so the identities hold over $\mathbb Q$ as well.

**The ascent decomposition (4): character comparison.** Let $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm{S}(y)$ for all $y<xs$ (so also $\mathrm{S}(x)$, and $\mathrm{S}(s)$ when $x\ne e$); by steps 4.1 and 5.1 decompose $M=B_xB_s=\bigoplus_{w,e}B_w^R(e)^{m_{w,e}}$ in $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$. By [F4] and step 5.1, $h_\Delta(M)=h_\Delta(B_x)h_\Delta(B_s)=\underline H_x\underline H_s$ (with $h_\Delta(B_e)=1$ in the case $x=e$), and by [F6] $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}\mu_y\underline H_y$ in the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis, where $\mu_y=\mu(y,x)$ if $y<x$ and $ys<y$, and $\mu_y=0$ otherwise; all other coefficients vanish. On the other hand $h_\Delta(M)=\sum_{w,e}m_{w,e}v^e\underline H_w$ because under $\mathrm{S}(w)$ the character of $B_w^R(e)$ is $v^e\underline H_w$. Comparing the two expansions in the basis $\{v^e\underline H_w\}$ of the free $A$-module $H\otimes_A A[v^{\pm1}]$, using that the $\underline H_w$ form an $A$-basis, yields $m_{xs,0}=1$, $m_{xs,e}=0$ for $e\ne0$, and $\sum_e m_{y,e}v^e=\mu_y$ for every $y<xs$.

**No shifts on the lower summands.** For $y<xs$ we have $S(y)$, so $h_\Delta(B_y)=\underline H_y$ and $h_
abla(B_y)=d(\underline H_y)=\underline H_y$, while $h_
abla(M)=h_
abla(B_x)h_
abla(B_s)=\underline H_x\underline H_s$ by [F4] and step 5.1; by [F7] together with the symmetry of the standard pairing $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(B_y,M)=\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_sangle=\langle\underline H_x\underline H_s,\underline H_yangle=\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(M,B_y)$. Expanding $\underline H_y=\sum_u p_{u,y}H_u$ and $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\sum_u c_uH_u$ in the normalized standard basis, and using [F6], this polynomial equals $\sum_u p_{u,y}\,c_u$ with $c_u\in\mathbb Z[v]$ and $p_{u,y}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, hence lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$; therefore $\operatorname{Hom}^j(B_y,M)=\operatorname{Hom}^j(M,B_y)=0$ for $j<0$. A summand $B_y(e)$ with $e>0$ would give a nonzero inclusion $B_y(e)	o M$ of degree $0$, hence a nonzero element of $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y(e),M)=\operatorname{Hom}^{-e}(B_y,M)$ in negative degree $-e<0$, a contradiction; a summand with $e<0$ would give a nonzero projection $M	o B_y(e)$ of degree $0$, hence a nonzero element of $\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y(e))=\operatorname{Hom}^{e}(M,B_y)$ in negative degree $e<0$, again a contradiction. Hence $m_{y,e}=0$ for $e
e0$ and every $y<xs$.

**The ascent decomposition, conclusion.** By steps 6.1 and 7.1, $M=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y(0)^{a_y}$ with $a_y:=m_{y,0}$ nonnegative integers, and the character identity of step 6.1 gives $a_y=\mu_y$ for every $y<xs$; the top summand $B_{xs}$ occurs exactly once.

**The descent case.** Let $xs<x$ and assume $S(x)$; by the right-descent clause of the multiplication formula [F6], $\underline H_x\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$, and by the same decomposition-and-character comparison as in step 6.1 we write $B_xB_s=\bigoplus_{w,e}B_w^R(e)^{m_{w,e}}$ and equate $h_\Delta(B_xB_s)=h_\Delta(B_x)h_\Delta(B_s)=\sum_{w,e}m_{w,e}v^e\underline H_w$ with $(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$; since the $\underline H_w$ form a basis and $v^e\underline H_w$ equals a term of $(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$ only for $w=x$, the multiplicities satisfy $m_{x,1}=m_{x,-1}=1$ and $m_{w,e}=0$ otherwise, so $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$.

**Conclusion.** Step 3.1 proves the indecomposability and locality in (1), and step 4.2 the assertion under $S(w)$; step 4.1 proves (2); step 5.1 proves (3); steps 8.1 and 8.2 prove both parts of (4). No positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials is assumed, no shift of a lower summand is produced, and no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: Every bimodule in the statement is one of the indecomposables of the finite type-A category or a product with a generator, and the decompositions displayed in steps 8.1 and 8.2 have no empty indexing family attached to them.

boundaries.evidence: Vanishing multiplicities are explicitly admissible: step 8.1 produces multiplicities a_y >= 0 and allows a_y = 0, and the phrase excluding further summands in step 8.2 is the assertion that the remaining multiplicities are zero.

Unit multiplicity is tracked twice: the top summand B_xs appears with multiplicity one in step 8.1, and the base case of that ascent decomposition with x of length zero is the bare product B_s handled by the same formula.

The descent situation, in which no new label appears, is treated separately in step 8.2 by the shifted split B_xB_s = B_x(1) + B_x(-1); the character comparison of steps 6.1 and 7.1 is what rules out hidden shifts in the ascent case.

Degree ends are controlled: steps 7.1 and 8.1 show every lower summand occurs without internal shift, and the degree-zero endomorphism space computed from step 2.1 through step 4.2 is the bottom-degree input of the locality statement.

Choice-free: step 1.1 selects a finite presentation of a finitely generated module over the Noetherian ring, and step 4.1 works with the finite list of indecomposable labels of the symmetric group; no infinite choice occurs.

boundaries.reason: The lemma is a conjunction of an indecomposability clause, a labelling clause and two decomposition clauses; none of them is stated as a biconditional needing a direction proof.
No reverse direction is stated: the four clauses impose conclusions from the character hypothesis rather than equivalence of two conditions.
