**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad
   \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad
   \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,
the simple reflections $s_i$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and recall that $R$ is
a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule and that shifts are defined as in
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]. For $1\le i\le n-1$ put
$$B_i:=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1),$$
the balanced tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]])
of the $(R,R^{s_i})$-bimodule $R$ with the $(R^{s_i},R)$-bimodule $R$, equipped
with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.

**The two outer actions.** The left $R$-action is $r'(r\otimes r'')=r'r\otimes r''$
and the right $R$-action is $(r\otimes r'')r'=r\otimes r''r'$; both descend to
the balanced tensor product, they commute, they are homogeneous of degree $0$,
and they satisfy $R$-linearity on the relevant side, so $B_i$ is a graded
$(R,R)$-bimodule over $R^{s_i}$-balanced tensors. Explicitly, the $(R,R)$-bimodule
$B_i$ is generated by the two elements $1\otimes1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$, which
are homogeneous of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ respectively: $\alpha_i$ is a
degree-$2$ element of $R$ and the external shift moves degrees by $-1$.

**Elementary structure.** Since $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q$, we have the
decomposition $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ (the averaging idempotent
$\tfrac12(1+s_i)$ and its complement), so as a graded left $R$-module and again
as a graded right $R$-module
$$B_i\cong R(-1)\oplus R(1),$$
and $B_i$ is finite free of rank two on each side. The Demazure operator
$\partial_i$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]] is
$R^{s_i}$-linear and surjective onto $R^{s_i}$, and
$\partial_i(\alpha_i h)=2h$ for $h\in R^{s_i}$,
a fact used when the exact sequences of $B_i$ are displayed later on this page.

**Small $n$.** For $n=0$ or $n=1$ there are no simple reflections and no
$B_i$. The only word is the empty word, with bimodule $R$; the additive graded
Bott–Samelson category contains all finite direct sums of shifts of $R$ and
all degree-zero bimodule maps between them.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad
   \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad
   \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Equivalently, $w\rho$ is positive on $\alpha_i^\vee$ exactly when $s_iw$ is
longer than $w$, so the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The bottom degree of $B_x^R$ is $-\ell(x)$ and its
top degree is $+\ell(x)$; on a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

**The setting.** Keep $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the
place-permutation action of $S_n$, the balanced roots
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$ with $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$ and the
graded $(R,R)$-bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]; recall that
$1\otimes1\in B_i$ has degree $-1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ has degree $1$, that
$B_i$ is generated as an $(R,R)$-bimodule by $1\otimes1$, and that $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ with
$s_i(\alpha_i)=-\alpha_i$
([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]],
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]).

**The positive generator complex.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ let $F_i$ be the
bounded cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i:=\bigl[\;B_i\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_i\ }R(1)\;\bigr],$$
with $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$, $R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and
all other terms zero, where $\varepsilon_i:B_i\to R(1)$ is the
multiplication map $\varepsilon_i(r\otimes r')=rr'$, i.e. the degree-zero
bimodule map determined by $\varepsilon_i(1\otimes1)=1$ and
$\varepsilon_i(1\otimes\alpha_i)=\alpha_i$.

**The negative generator complex.** Let $F_i^{-1}$ be the bounded cochain
complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i^{-1}:=\bigl[\;R(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta_i\ }B_i\;\bigr],$$
with $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$, $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$ and
all other terms zero, where $\eta_i:R(-1)\to B_i$ is the bimodule map
$\eta_i(1)=\alpha_i\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_i$.

**Well-definedness of the differentials.** The map $\varepsilon_i$ descends
from the multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$ because
$\varepsilon_i(ra\otimes r')=rar'=\varepsilon_i(r\otimes ar')$ for $a\in R^{s_i}$
and $R$ is commutative; it is left and right $R$-linear and homogeneous of
degree zero, since $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ matches the degrees $-1$ of $B_i$ and of
the generator of $R(1)$, and $1\otimes\alpha_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ matches the
degree $1=\deg(\alpha_i)-1$ on both sides. For $\eta_i$, the bimodule map
$R\to B_i$ sending $1$ to the class of $x_i-x'_{i+1}$ is well defined: the
products $(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_i-x'_i)$ and
$(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_{i+1}-x'_{i+1})$ vanish in $B_i$ by the explicit computation
of GKS Lemma 3.8, while for $a\notin\{i,i+1\}$ the factor $x_a-x'_a$ is already
a defining relation of $B_i$, so the element annihilates the kernel ideal of the
multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$, and the assignment $1\mapsto x_i-x'_{i+1}$
extends to a well-defined $R$-bimodule map. The value of that map at $1$ times
the unit $2\varepsilon_i$ is $\eta_i(1)$, because
$$1\otimes(x_i-x_{i+1})+(x_i-x_{i+1})\otimes1=2(x_i-x'_{i+1})$$
in $B_i$ (GKS Lemma 3.8, using $x_i+x_{i+1}=x'_i+x'_{i+1}$) and
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$; a unit multiple of a well-defined
bimodule map is a well-defined bimodule map, so $\eta_i$ is well defined. Its
value $\eta_i(1)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$, matching the degree of
$1\in R(-1)$, so $\eta_i$ is a degree-zero bimodule map. Both complexes are
concentrated in two adjacent cohomological
degrees, so $d^2=0$ holds trivially and each of $F_i,F_i^{-1}$ is a bounded
cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules in the sense of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]].

**Size and consequences.** The bimodules $R$, $R(1)$ and $R(-1)$ are free of
rank one on both sides and $B_i$ is free of rank two on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], the bases
being $\{1\otimes1,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ on the left and
$\{1\otimes1,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ on the right). Every term of $F_i$ and of
$F_i^{-1}$ is therefore finite free, hence finite graded projective, as a left
$R$-module and as an underlying right $R$-module. Applying
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]]
with the commutative ring $\mathbb Q$ and $A=B=R$: the signed totalization with
$F_i$ is an exact triangulated functor on bounded complexes of finite graded
projective $R$-modules, preserves quasi-isomorphisms between bounded complexes,
and descends to the derived tensor functor $F_i\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}-$ on
$D^b(R\text{-grmod})$; the same statements hold with $F_i^{-1}$ in place of
$F_i$. The right-tensor construction $-\otimes_RF_i$ is defined separately by
signed totalization, and its derived version uses the same two-sided
freeness. Commutativity of $R$ does not assert a symmetry between tensor
products of arbitrary $(R,R)$-bimodules.

**Recorded convention.** The complex $F_i$ is the library normalization of
Rouquier's positive complex $F_s=[A\otimes_{A^s}A\to A]$, in which $A$ sits in
degree $1$ and the differential is multiplication: in the library external
shift $(r)$ with $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$ one has $F_i=T_i(1)$ and
$F_i^{-1}\cong T_i^{-1}(-1)$ for the GKS complexes
$T_i=[B_i(-1)\to R]$, $T_i^{-1}=[R\to B_i(1)]$ of formula (3.3). The GKS negative differential sends $1$ to
$x_i-x'_{i+1}$, whereas ours is $2\varepsilon_i$ times that map.
The chain isomorphism $F_i^{-1}\to T_i^{-1}(-1)$ is multiplication by
$2\varepsilon_i$ in degree $-1$ and the identity in degree $0$.
The internal shifts cancel in inverse pairs and agree on the two sides of
each positive braid relation. The sign $\varepsilon_i$
in $\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$, and with it the sign of $\eta_i$, is
a unit of $\mathbb Q$; the homotopy classes of the complexes do not depend on
the choice of balanced root.

**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

**Convention for comparison.** The library's positive generator $F_i$ is
Rouquier's $F_{s_i}=[A\otimes_{A^{s_i}}A\to A]$ with the library external shift
$(1)$ on both terms, after giving the polynomial variables degree $2$:
$$F_i=[(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)(1)\longrightarrow R(1)].$$
Rouquier's negative complex of §3.2.4 becomes $F_i^{-1}$ after doubling
internal degrees and shifting the whole complex by $(-1)$, up to the unit
scalar coming from the root normalization. As recorded in
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], the
complexes of Rouquier, Gorsky–Kivinen–Simental, Khovanov and Elias–Krasner
differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
comparison with those sources is read through the dictionary recorded there.
The empty word corresponds to the trivial braid and to the identity functor.

derivations.claim: **The single-factor identity.** Let $s$ be a simple reflection with root $\alpha=\alpha_s$, let $\mathrm{Br}(b):=bc_s$ on $B_s$, and let $\sigma\in S$. For every $b\in B_s$ one has $\sigma\cdot b=b\cdot(s\sigma)+\partial_s(\sigma)\,\mathrm{Br}(b)$. Indeed both sides are right $S$-linear in $b$, so it suffices to check the two basis elements: for $b=c_{\mathrm{id}}$ the identity is the rule $r\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot sr+\partial_s(r)c_s$ of [F1] with $r=\sigma$, and for $b=c_s$ it reads $\sigma\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot s\sigma+\partial_s(\sigma)c_s\alpha_s$, which is $c_s\sigma=c_s(s\sigma+\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma))$ and holds because $\sigma-s\sigma=\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma)$ and $c_s$ commutes with $S$.

**Iteration over the letters proves (1).** For the empty expression $m=0$ the bimodule is $\mathrm{BS}(\varnothing)=S$, the sum over the letters is empty, and left multiplication by $\rho$ equals right multiplication by $x^{-1}\rho=\rho$ because $S$ is commutative, so (a) holds; assume therefore $m\ge1$. Let $b=b_1\cdots b_m$ be a tensor monomial with $b_i\in B_{s_i}$, and apply step 1.1 at the first factor with $\sigma=\rho$: since left multiplication by $\rho$ of the tensor acts on the first factor, $\rho\cdot b=\bigl(\rho\cdot b_1\bigr)b_2\cdots b_m=b_1\cdots b_m\cdot(s_1\rho)+\partial_{s_1}(\rho)\,\mathrm{Br}_1(b)$, where the first summand is the tensor with the element $b_1\cdot(s_1\rho)\in B_{s_1}$ in the first slot; applying step 1.1 to $b_1\cdot(s_1\rho)$ with $\sigma=s_1\rho$ would return the same expression, while reading the first summand as an element of the tensor product carrying the leftover $\sigma_1:=s_1\rho$ allows the same expansion at the second factor, producing the coefficient $(s_1\rho)(\alpha_{s_2}^\vee)$ and the leftover $\sigma_2:=s_2s_1\rho$. Iterating $m$ times produces exactly the sum $\sum_{i=1}^m(s_{i-1}\cdots s_1\rho)(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)\,\mathrm{Br}_i(b)$ together with the final leftover $s_m\cdots s_1\rho=x^{-1}\rho$ acting by right multiplication on the last slot; using $\mathrm{Br}_i=\chi_i\circ\varphi_i$ this is the displayed identity. Since both sides are degree-zero endomorphisms and the tensor monomials span $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$, the identity holds on all of $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The covariance identity.** For all $b,b'\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ and all $i$ one has $\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_i b'\rangle=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$. It suffices to check on tensor monomials $b=b_1\cdots b_m$, $b'=b'_1\cdots b'_m$: the left side is $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots(b_ib'_ic_{s_i})\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)c_{s_i}\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)$, and since the $c$-basis is multiplicative, $\mu(b_i)c_{s_i}=\mu(b_i)\mu(c_{s_i})$, so this equals $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\chi_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$, using $\operatorname{Tr}\circ\chi_i=\operatorname{Tr}_i$ and the multiplicativity of the ring structure.

**The rescaled form identity (b).** With $\varphi=\sum_i\varphi_i$ and $\langle-,-\rangle'=\bigoplus_i\langle-,-\rangle_i'$, the direct sum decomposition is orthogonal, so for all $b,b'$ one has $\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'=\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$; substituting step 2.2 gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle=\langle b,\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$, and substituting the factorization of step 2.1 gives $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle-\langle b,b'\cdot x^{-1}\rho\rangle$. The second summand is $-\langle b,b'\rangle\,x^{-1}\rho$ by right $S$-linearity of the form, and it vanishes after reduction because $x^{-1}\rho$ has positive degree; hence $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle_{\overline{\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)}}=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'$ for $b,b'$ in the reduced module, as claimed in (b).

**Positivity for reduced words and the vanished remainder (c).** Let $\underline x$ be reduced. For each $i$, the prefix $w_i:=s_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ has length $i-1$ and $s_iw_i$ has length $i$; the descent criterion [F3] therefore gives $\gamma_i=(w_i\rho)(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)>0$. All rescalings are by strictly positive real numbers, so no sign in a definite form changes; and $x^{-1}\rho$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree $2$ whose right multiplication lands in $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)S_+$, which becomes zero after reduction, so the remainder vanishes on the reduced module. This proves (c).

**Identification with the Rouquier differential (d).** By [F4] the first differential of the Rouquier complex is the signed sum, over the letters, of the maps $\varphi_i$ from the cohomological degree $0$ term $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ to the degree $1$ term $\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)$, and its dual maps decompose the generator $c_{s_i}$ back, i.e. are the maps $\chi_i$ up to the fixed shift and Koszul signs. Composing the differential with the rescaled dual maps $\gamma_i\chi_i$ and summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_i$, which by step 2.1 equals left multiplication by $\rho$ modulo the right-multiplication remainder that vanishes on the reduced module by step 4.1. Hence left multiplication by $\rho$ on the reduced Bott-Samelson module factors, up to the positive rescalings $\gamma_i$, as the composite $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)\xrightarrow{\ \gamma\chi\ }\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(2)$ built from the first Rouquier differential and its dual; the sign conventions of [F4] fix the composite to be exactly $\rho\cdot(-)$ up to the fixed Koszul signs of the two-term totalization in this normalization and the positive rescalings $\gamma_i$ of step 4.1. This proves (d) and completes the lemma; no positivity of characters and no character conjecture is used.

boundaries.evidence: The empty expression is discharged at the start of step 2.1: for m = 0 the bimodule is the unit S, the letter sum is empty, and left multiplication by rho equals right multiplication by x^{-1}rho because the polynomial ring is commutative, so clause (a) holds; the remaining clauses then reduce to the same identity.

Two distinct zeros are handled: the cross terms between different summands vanish by the orthogonality recorded in step 3.1, and the remainder term obtained by right multiplication by the leftover polynomial is shown in step 4.1 to become zero after passing to the reduced module.

The single-factor case is the rank-one identity proved in step 1.1 and is the first case of the iteration in step 2.1; for the reduced one-letter word its scaling factor is the positive value produced by the descent criterion in step 4.1.

No reducedness is assumed for clauses (a) and (b): step 2.1 gives the factorization and step 3.1 the rescaled form identity for every expression, and step 4.1 names the exact two places where a reduced word is needed, positivity of the scalings and vanishing of the remainder.

The ends of the letter list are pinned down: step 1.1 treats the first factor, step 2.1 carries the leftover through all letters, and step 4.1 handles the final leftover x^{-1}rho separately from the sum.
Choice-free: all identities are verified on tensor monomials built from the fixed two-element right bases of the finitely many factors, as described in step 2.1 and step 2.2.

boundaries.reason: Clauses (a) through (d) are displayed identities together with a positivity statement; the lemma never asserts that two conditions are equivalent, so no forward direction exists.
There is no converse to prove: the factorization of left multiplication by rho is an identity up to positive rescaling, not one half of an equivalence.

citations.quote:
**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here
$d=\ell(x)$; $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on
$\overline{B_x^R}$, and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the Hodge-Riemann relations
with the standard sign for this normalized form. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ for the restriction of the
intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over a field of characteristic not $2$. Every symmetric bilinear form $B$ on $V$ admits a basis whose distinct vectors are pairwise orthogonal for $B$.

Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space is congruent to exactly one normal form

$$\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r),\qquad p+q+r=\dim V.$$

Equivalently, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries are independent of the diagonalizing basis.

Let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and write $q(v):=B(v,v)$. The form is **positive definite** when $q(v)>0$ for every $v\ne0$, and **negative definite** when $q(v)<0$ for every $v\ne0$. The same terminology applies to the associated quadratic form.

Suppose a basis gives a diagonal matrix with $p$ positive diagonal entries, $q$ negative diagonal entries, and $r$ zero entries. Its **inertia** is the triple $(p,q,r)$, its **rank** is $p+q$, and its **signature** is $p-q$. Sylvester's law of inertia proves that this triple is independent of the diagonalizing basis, and therefore justifies the notation.

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on an $n$-dimensional vector space $V$, and let $\mathcal B=(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis. The **matrix of $B$ in $\mathcal B$** is

$$[B]_{\mathcal B}:=(B(v_i,v_j))_{i,j<n}.$$

For coordinate columns $x=[u]_{\mathcal B}$ and $y=[v]_{\mathcal B}$, one has $B(u,v)=x^{\mathsf T}[B]_{\mathcal B}y$.

The **left radical** and **right radical** are

$$\operatorname{rad}_L(B):=\{u:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\},\qquad \operatorname{rad}_R(B):=\{v:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}.$$

The **rank of $B$** is the rank of the associated map $B^\flat:V\to V^*$, $B^\flat(u)(v)=B(u,v)$. The form is **nondegenerate** when both radicals are zero. In finite dimension this is equivalent to $B^\flat$ being an isomorphism, and also to $[B]_{\mathcal B}$ being invertible.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here
$d=\ell(x)$; $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on
$\overline{B_x^R}$, and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the Hodge-Riemann relations
with the standard sign for this normalized form. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ for the restriction of the
intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

derivations.claim: **One step of the decomposition.** Under hL the map $L^{i+2}:H^{-i-2}\to H^{i+2}$ is an isomorphism, so for every $a\in H^{-i}$ there is $b\in H^{-i-2}$ with $L^{i+1}a=L^{i+2}b$; then $a-Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, and hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}+L\,H^{-i-2}$. The sum is direct: if $Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, then $0=L^{i+1}(Lb)=L^{i+2}b$ and injectivity of $L^{i+2}$ gives $b=0$; hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,H^{-i-2}$.

**Iteration and the primitive decomposition (a).** Iterating step 1.1 gives $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,P_L^{-i-2}\oplus L^2P_L^{-i-4}\oplus\cdots=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$, the sum terminating because $H^{-m}=0$ for $m>d$; reindexing by the lowest primitive degree gives $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$, since every string $L^kP_L^{-i}$ lies in degrees between $-i$ and $i$, so $k\le i$ for nonzero contributions. This proves (a).

**Orthogonality (b).** Let $p\in P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ and $q\in P_L^{-(i+2l)}$ with $k<l$ and consider $a=L^kp$, $b=L^lq$ in $H^{-i}$. Using symmetry of $L$ repeatedly, $(a,b)_L^{-i}=\langle L^kp,L^{i+l}q\rangle=\langle p,L^{i+k+l}q\rangle$, and the exponent satisfies $i+k+l\ge i+2k+1$; since $L^{i+2k+1}p=0$, the pairing vanishes. Hence distinct strings are orthogonal for the Lefschetz form, as claimed.

**Non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms is equivalent to hL (c).** For fixed $i$, the Lefschetz form at degree $-i$ is the composite of the linear map $L^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ with the perfect pairing $H^i\times H^{-i}\to\mathbb R$ given by the form; the latter is an isomorphism $H^i\to(H^{-i})^*$ by non-degeneracy of $\langle-,-\rangle$ [F1]. Hence the Lefschetz form is non-degenerate if and only if $L^i$ is an isomorphism; this holds simultaneously for all $i\ge0$ exactly when hL holds, and for $i>d$ both sides are zero by [F1] ($\dim H^i=\dim H^{-i}=0$). This proves (c).

**Signature formula (d).** Assume hL and the standard-sign definiteness on primitives. The orthogonal decomposition of step 3.1 expresses the form on $H^{-i}$ as an orthogonal sum of the forms $(p,q)\mapsto\langle p,L^{i+2k}q\rangle$ on the primitive spaces $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$; each of these is definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}$ by HR, and its own inertia is therefore $(\dim P,0,0)$ or $(0,\dim P,0)$ according to that sign. Sylvester's law [F2] makes the signature of the orthogonal sum the sum of the summand signatures, giving the displayed formula. Conversely, assume hL and the signature formula for all $i$; descending from the bottom degree, the formula determines the signature of the primitive form on $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ after the signatures of the higher-degree primitive spaces are known, and by non-degeneracy [F2] the only possible signatures are $\pm\dim$, so each primitive form is definite with the stated sign; this recovers HR. This proves (d).

**Stable subspaces (e).** Let $V\subseteq H$ be $L$-stable with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$. Since $L^i$ is injective on $H$ (hL), its restriction to $V$ is injective, and the dimension symmetry makes it an isomorphism onto $V^i$; hence $V$ satisfies hL for the restricted operator and form. Its primitive spaces are $P_V^{-i}=V^{-i}\cap P_L^{-i}$, because the kernel of $L^{i+1}$ on $V^{-i}$ is the intersection with the kernel on $H^{-i}$; the restricted Lefschetz form on $P_V^{-i}$ is the restriction of the ambient definite primitive form, hence definite with the ambient sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$. The primitive decomposition of $V$ from (a) then shows, exactly as in step 5.1, that the restricted form on $V$ is an orthogonal sum of definite blocks, hence non-degenerate, and that its signs are the ambient signs; if the lowest nonzero degree of $V$ equals $-d$, then the ambient sign formula is also the standard sign of $V$. This proves (e) and completes the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: For the zero space every summand in the decompositions of step 2.1 and step 4.1 is zero and the assertions hold vacuously; the string sum of step 2.1 is finite and terminates once the degree leaves the range of H.

Zero operators and zero pairings are covered: step 1.1 subtracts Lb, which may already be zero, to reach a primitive vector, and the strings L^k P^{-(i+2k)} are zero once the degree drops below the lowest degree, which is why step 2.1 terminates.
A length-one string is the k = 0 term of the decomposition in step 2.1, and the direct summand P_L^{-i} constructed in step 1.1 is exactly the primitive part of the degree -i piece.

Degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms is not assumed away but characterized: step 4.1 exhibits the form as a composite with the perfect pairing, so it degenerates precisely when L^i fails to be an isomorphism, which is the content of the exactly-when clause.

Both grading ends are used: the decomposition of step 2.1 terminates at the top degree, and the signature formula proved in step 5.1 is anchored at the lowest nonzero degree where the primitive form is the whole space.
Choice-free: the decompositions are taken in finite-dimensional real vector spaces and the complements are built from finitely many vectors in step 1.1, so no infinite selection is required.

Forward direction of the exactly-when clause: step 4.1 writes the Lefschetz form at degree -i as the composite of L^i with a perfect pairing, so non-degeneracy forces L^i injective, and the dimension symmetry recorded there upgrades this to an isomorphism, which is hL.

Reverse direction: if L^i is an isomorphism then the composite form of step 4.1 is a perfect pairing, so every Lefschetz form is non-degenerate; step 3.1 supplies the orthogonal decomposition used to recognize the non-degenerate direct sum.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad
   \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad
   \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. **The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.
