Let $B$ be a bilinear form on an $n$-dimensional vector space $V$, and let $\mathcal B=(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis. The **matrix of $B$ in $\mathcal B$** is

$$[B]_{\mathcal B}:=(B(v_i,v_j))_{i,j<n}.$$

For coordinate columns $x=[u]_{\mathcal B}$ and $y=[v]_{\mathcal B}$, one has $B(u,v)=x^{\mathsf T}[B]_{\mathcal B}y$.

The **left radical** and **right radical** are

$$\operatorname{rad}_L(B):=\{u:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\},\qquad \operatorname{rad}_R(B):=\{v:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}.$$

The **rank of $B$** is the rank of the associated map $B^\flat:V\to V^*$, $B^\flat(u)(v)=B(u,v)$. The form is **nondegenerate** when both radicals are zero. In finite dimension this is equivalent to $B^\flat$ being an isomorphism, and also to $[B]_{\mathcal B}$ being invertible.

derivations.claim: **Invariant forms and degree-zero Hom.** By [F1] an invariant form on $B_x^R$ is the same as a degree-zero bimodule map $B_x^R\to D\,B_x^R$, so the space of invariant forms is $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_x^R,D\,B_x^R)$; it is an $\mathbb R$-module under left multiplication on the output. Under $\mathrm{S}(x)$ we have $D\,B_x^R\cong B_x^R$ and $\operatorname{End}^0(B_x^R)=\mathbb R$ by [F2], so this space is one-dimensional over $\mathbb R$.

**Orthogonality of isotypic components.** Let $B=\bigoplus_zB_z^{R,m_z}$ with $\mathrm{S}(z)$ for all $z$ and let $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ be a symmetric invariant form, non-degenerate or not. For $z\ne y$, $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_z^R,D\,B_y^R)=0$ because the two sides are non-isomorphic indecomposables with local endomorphism algebras [F2]; hence the form pairs the $B_z$-isotypic component $V_z\otimes B_z^R$ (with $V_z$ the real multiplicity space) orthogonally to the $B_y$-isotypic component for $y\ne z$.

**Existence of a non-degenerate form and uniqueness.** The restriction of the intersection form of a Bott-Samelson bimodule to $B_x^R$ is invariant and non-degenerate by [F3] and [F1], so the one-dimensional space of step 1.1 contains a non-degenerate form. Every other invariant form is a scalar multiple of it by dimension, and a nonzero scalar multiple of an isomorphism is again an isomorphism, hence non-degenerate; this proves (1).

**Multiplicity pairings (4).** On the isotypic component $V_z\otimes B_z^R$, every invariant form is of the shape $\langle v\otimes b,v'\otimes b'\rangle=Q_z(v,v')\langle b,b'\rangle_z$ for a unique symmetric bilinear form $Q_z$ on the finite-dimensional real space $V_z$: invariance in $b$ and in $v$ forces the factorisation, using that the normalized form on $B_z^R$ is the unique invariant form up to scalar by (1). The full form on $B$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the forms $Q_z\otimes\langle-,-\rangle_z$, and it is non-degenerate exactly when every $Q_z$ is nonsingular. By [F5] each nonsingular symmetric $Q_z$ admits an orthogonal decomposition into one-dimensional definite blocks $Q_z=\bigoplus_\alpha q_{z,\alpha}$, giving a splitting of the isotypic component into orthogonal indecomposable copies $B_z^R$ with restricted forms the scalar multiples $q_{z,\alpha}\langle-,-\rangle_z$; this proves the existence of the orthogonal isotypic decomposition and completes (4).

**Positivity of the comparison scalar.** Let $\underline x$ be a reduced expression and $B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ an embedding as a direct summand; write $\langle-,-\rangle_{\mathrm{BS}}$ for the restricted form and $\langle-,-\rangle_x$ for the normalized intrinsic form. By (1) both are non-zero invariant forms on $B_x^R$, so $\langle-,-\rangle_{\mathrm{BS}}=c\,\langle-,-\rangle_x$ for a unique non-zero real scalar $c$. The bottom space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ is one-dimensional: by the $\nabla$-character of $B_x$ its lowest degree occurs with multiplicity one [F2, F3], and any embedding induces an isomorphism of this line onto the bottom line of the Bott-Samelson module. The normalized intrinsic form has $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle_x=1$ by its normalization, while $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle_{\mathrm{BS}}>0$ by [F3]; hence $c>0$. This proves (2).

**HR comparison (3).** The two forms differ by the positive scalar $c$ of step 3.1, so for every degree the associated Lefschetz forms differ by the same positive scalar $c$; definiteness and its sign are therefore the same for both, and the primitive subspaces coincide because they are kernels of the same operator $L_0$. Hence $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ for the intrinsic form holds if and only if $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ holds for the restricted form of any fixed embedding, which is the equivalence with $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ in the sense of [F4]; positivity of $c$ ensures the standard signs are not altered.

**Conclusion.** Steps 1.1-2.1 prove (1), steps 3.1-4.1 prove (2) and (3), and steps 1.2 and 2.2 prove (4). The argument uses the Hom formula and the positivity of the bottom Lefschetz form, and does not assume any positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement concerns the fixed indecomposable B_x and a finite isotypic decomposition of a fixed bimodule; no empty family of summands or empty indexing set occurs in its clauses.

boundaries.evidence: The zero form and zero scalar multiples are classified: step 2.1 shows the space of invariant forms on B_x is spanned by one non-degenerate element, so the zero form is the unique degenerate invariant form, and every nonzero scalar multiple stays non-degenerate.

Two one-dimensional phenomena carry the proof: the space of invariant forms on B_x is one-dimensional by steps 1.1 and 2.1, and the multiplicity-one top summand is compared through the positive scalar computed in step 3.1.

Degenerate forms are classified rather than excluded: step 1.2 shows any invariant form on a sum of isotypic components is an orthogonal sum, and step 2.2 proves non-degeneracy holds precisely when every multiplicity-space pairing Q_z is nonsingular.

The comparison of normalizations is anchored at the bottom primitive: step 3.1 evaluates both forms on the lowest-degree class and identifies the ratio, and step 4.1 transfers the same positive scalar to the Lefschetz form in every degree.
Choice-free: the argument uses the Hom formula for finitely generated graded free modules in steps 1.1 and 1.2 and never selects from an infinite set of indecomposables.

Forward direction of clause (3): if the intrinsic form satisfies HR then the embedded intersection form, being a positive multiple c of it by steps 3.1 and 4.1, satisfies HR as well, since positive rescaling preserves both the isomorphisms and the definiteness signs.

Reverse direction: the embedded form differs from the intrinsic one by the positive scalar of step 3.1, so its HR signs are transferred back by step 4.1; positivity is what rules out a sign change in the comparison.

citations.quote: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $X^\bullet$ be a cochain complex in an additive category with an
invertible-block decomposition
$d^n=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&\varphi\end{pmatrix}:A\oplus U\to B\oplus V$ and
Schur complement $\bar d=a-b\varphi^{-1}c$, as in
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]], and let
$\bar X^\bullet$ be the candidate reduction. Let $K$ be the two-term cochain
complex with $K^n=U$, $K^{n+1}=V$, $K^j=0$ for $j\notin\{n,n+1\}$ and
differential $d_K^n=\varphi$; write $\bar X\oplus K$ for the degreewise
biproduct.

1. The cochain map $T:X^\bullet\to\bar X^\bullet\oplus K$ with components
   $$T^j=1\ (j\notin\{n,n+1\}),\qquad T^n=R^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \varphi^{-1}c&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^{n+1}=L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\varphi^{-1}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$$
   is an isomorphism of cochain complexes, with inverse the cochain map $T^{-1}$
   whose components are $1$ in degrees $j\notin\{n,n+1\}$, $R$ in degree $n$ and
   $L^{-1}$ in degree $n+1$.
2. $K$ is contractible, with contracting homotopy $k^{n+1}=\varphi^{-1}:V\to U$
   and $k^j=0$ for $j\ne n+1$.
3. $X^\bullet$ and $\bar X^\bullet$ are homotopy equivalent: the projection
   $\tilde p:\bar X\oplus K\to\bar X$ and the inclusion
   $\tilde\imath:\bar X\to\bar X\oplus K$ satisfy
   $\tilde p\tilde\imath=1$ and $1-\tilde\imath\tilde p=d\tilde h+\tilde h d$
   for the homotopy $\tilde h$ vanishing except in degree $n+1$, where
   $\tilde h^{n+1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&\varphi^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, so that
   $p:=\tilde pT$ and $\imath:=T^{-1}\tilde\imath$ are homotopy inverse cochain
   maps.
4. The construction is a chain isomorphism followed by deletion of a
   contractible summand: it does not identify $X^\bullet$ with
   $\bar X^\bullet$ before that summand is split off, and in general $X^\bullet$
   and $\bar X^\bullet$ do not even have the same objects.

derivations.claim: **Endomorphism algebras are finite-dimensional with residue field $\mathbb R$.** For indecomposables $X=B_x^R(d)$, $Y=B_y^R(e)$ the graded Hom space is finite free over $S$ in each degree and its degree-zero part is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb R$; hence for a finite direct sum $M=\bigoplus_aX_a$ the algebra $\operatorname{End}(M)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb R$ in degree zero, with block matrix entries $\operatorname{Hom}^0(X_a,X_b)$. If $X\not\cong Y$ then $\operatorname{Hom}^0(X,Y)$ consists of non-units (a split injection or surjection would exhibit a common summand of two non-isomorphic indecomposables with local endomorphism rings), while $\operatorname{End}^0(X)$ is local with residue $\mathbb R$ by [F1]; the radical of $\operatorname{End}(M)$ is therefore the set of matrices whose every diagonal block is a non-unit, and $\operatorname{End}(M)/\operatorname{rad}$ is the product of the matrix algebras $\mathbb M_{m_{c}}(\mathbb R)$ over the isomorphism classes $c=(x,k)$ of summands. Because all these matrix algebras are simple over the field $\mathbb R$ and cross-class maps vanish, $\operatorname{End}(M)/\operatorname{rad}$ is a finite product of matrix algebras over $\mathbb R$, hence semisimple.

**Nilpotence of the radical and reflection of isomorphisms.** The radical of the finite-dimensional algebra $\operatorname{End}(M)$ is nilpotent, since it is contained in the set of elements $r$ such that $1-r$ is invertible in the finite-dimensional algebra: the descending chain of powers $\operatorname{rad}^{k}$ stabilizes in finite dimension, and the minimal-generator argument applied to a stable nonzero term forces it to be zero. If $q(f)$ is invertible in $\mathcal B^{ss}$, lift a two-sided inverse $g$; then $1-gf$ and $1-fg$ lie in $\operatorname{rad}\operatorname{End}$ of the relevant objects, and the finite geometric series $(1-(1-gf))^{-1}$ inverts $1-(1-gf)$, so $f$ is invertible. Hence $q$ reflects isomorphisms, and the simple classes of $\mathcal B^{ss}$ are the $B_x(k)$ with endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$; this proves (1).

**Minimal models exist (2), existence.** Let $F$ be a bounded complex; if $q(d^n)=0$ in every degree, $F$ is minimal and we are done. Otherwise some differential $d^n:F^n\to F^{n+1}$ has $q(d^n)\ne0$; writing $F^n,F^{n+1}$ as finite sums of shifted indecomposables, $q(d^n)$ has a nonzero matrix entry between summands of the same class $(x,k)$, because the simple objects of $\mathcal B^{ss}$ are the $B_x(k)$ and cross-class entries vanish by step 1.1. That entry is an invertible element of the local ring $\operatorname{End}^0(B_x^R(k))$, so the corresponding block of $d^n$ is invertible; [F3] applies and replaces $F$ by a homotopy equivalent complex with two fewer indecomposable summands. Repeating finitely many times produces a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence (a composite of the Gaussian-elimination homotopy equivalences), as claimed.

**Uniqueness of minimal models (2), uniqueness.** Let $f:F\to G$ be a homotopy equivalence between minimal complexes. Applying $q$ degreewise, $q(d_F)=0$ and $q(d_G)=0$, so $q(f)$ is a degreewise morphism of complexes with zero differentials, i.e. a degreewise map of graded $\mathcal B^{ss}$-modules; since $f$ is a homotopy equivalence and $q$ is additive, $q(f)$ is an isomorphism in the homotopy category of complexes over the semisimple category $\mathcal B^{ss}$, hence each $q(f^n)$ is an isomorphism. As $q$ reflects isomorphisms by step 2.1, each $f^n$ is an isomorphism, so $f$ is an isomorphism of complexes. This proves (2).

**Summands of perverse objects (3).** Let $M$ be p-split with a decomposition into shifts of perverse summands and let $M'$ be a direct summand of $M$; then $M'$ is a finite sum of shifted indecomposables $B_y^R(e)$ by [F1]. The character of $M$ is bar-invariant and equals $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\underline H_{x_\alpha}$ in the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis with all $c_\alpha$ nonnegative integers; expanding in the standard basis and using $\underline H_x=H_x+\sum_{y<x}p_{y,x}H_y$ with $p_{y,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ shows that every standard-basis coefficient of $\operatorname{ch}(M)$ lies in $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v]$. The standard coefficients of $\operatorname{ch}(M')$ are sums of nonnegative multiplicities of $M$, hence nonnegative Laurent polynomials whose sum with those of the complementary summand equals the coefficient of $\operatorname{ch}(M)$; a sum of nonnegative Laurent polynomials has no negative $v$-powers if the total has none, so the same holds for $\operatorname{ch}(M')$. Expand $\operatorname{ch}(M')=\sum_zf_z(v)\underline H_z$ with $f_z\in\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$; the standard coefficient of $H_y$ in $\operatorname{ch}(M')$ is $\sum_{z\ge y}f_zp_{y,z}$, and descending induction on the Bruhat order in $y$ using $p_{y,z}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $z>y$ shows $f_y\in\mathbb Z[v]$ for every $y$: the term $f_y\cdot1$ is the only contribution to the constant term among the $z\ge y$ contributions of $H_y$, and all others have positive $v$-valuation. Bar-invariance of $\operatorname{ch}(M')$ and of every $\underline H_z$ forces each $f_y$ to be fixed by $v\mapsto v^{-1}$; an element of $\mathbb Z[v]$ fixed by inversion is constant, $f_y=c_y\in\mathbb Z$. Finally $c_y$ equals the constant term of the standard coefficient of $H_y$ in $\operatorname{ch}(M')$, which is nonnegative. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(M')=\sum_yc_y\underline H_y$ with $c_y\ge0$ integers, so $M'$ is perverse; the p-split case follows by decomposing into indecomposables and applying the perverse case to each isotypic summand. This proves (3).

**Hom vanishing for perverse objects (4).** Let $M=\bigoplus_x(B_x^R)^{m_x}$, $N=\bigoplus_y(B_y^R)^{n_y}$ be perverse with all $m_x,n_y\ge0$ integers and no shifts, which is the form in which the character is a nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements; by [F1] the graded rank of $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)$ is $\langle\operatorname{ch}(M),d(\operatorname{ch}(N))\rangle=\sum_{x,y}m_xn_y(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)$ for the $A$-bilinear trace form, and by [F2] this equals $\sum_xm_xn_x(1+v\mathbb Z[v])+(\text{elements of }v\mathbb Z[v])\in\mathbb Z[v]$, a polynomial with nonnegative $v$-powers. A degree-zero map $M\to N(-i)$ is a degree-$(-i)$ map $M\to N$ in the internal grading, so its space is the degree-$(-i)$ part of $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)$; this vanishes for $i>0$ because the graded rank has no negative $v$-powers. This proves (4).

**Intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts (5).** Let $X=B_x^R(k)$ and $Y=B_y^R(l)$ be shifts of perverse summands of p-split objects. By the same computation as in step 6.1 with $m_x=n_y=1$, the graded rank of $\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)$ equals $v^{l-k}$ times the graded rank of $\operatorname{Hom}(B_x^R,B_y^R)$, and the latter lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$ because both characters are nonnegative integer combinations of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and the trace-form values $(\underline H_z,\underline H_w)$ lie in $\mathbb Z[v]$ with nonnegative $v$-powers by [F2]. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}^0(X,Y)=\operatorname{Hom}^{k-l}(B_x^R,B_y^R)=0$ unless $k-l\le0$, that is, every degree-zero morphism from $X$ to $Y$ satisfies $l\ge k$. Consequently every degree-zero morphism raises the internal shift parameter and maps the subobject $\tau_{\le j}M$ into $\tau_{\le j}M'$ for any morphism $f:M\to M'$ of p-split objects. Applying this to an isomorphism between two p-split decompositions of the same object and to its inverse shows that the two $\tau_{\le j}$ subobjects coincide, so the cuts are independent of the decomposition, and the containment just displayed is the functoriality. This proves (5).

**Minimal-model testing and triangle closure (6).** A minimal model is obtained from a complex by splitting off contractible two-term summands by [F3] and steps 3.1-4.1; since a contractible complex is isomorphic in the homotopy category to the zero complex and the cuts of a direct sum are the direct sums of the cuts, the bounds $\tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0$ and $F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)$ hold on a complex if and only if they hold on any minimal model. For closure under extensions, let $F'\to F\to F''\to$ be a distinguished triangle with $F',F''$ satisfying the $\ge0$ bounds; represent $F'$ and $F''$ by complexes with p-split terms obeying $\tau_{<-i}=0$, and represent $F$ by the mapping cone of $F''[-1]\to F'$, whose $i$-th term is $F'^i\oplus F''^{i-1}$; since $F''^{i-1}$ satisfies $\tau_{<-(i-1)}=0$ and $F'^i$ satisfies $\tau_{<-i}=0$, and $\tau_{<-i}\subseteq\tau_{<-(i-1)}$, the direct sum satisfies $\tau_{<-i}=0$, so $F\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. The same argument with the dual inequalities $k\ge i$ proves closure of $pK^b_{\le0}$; nothing in the argument uses minimality of the representatives, only the bounds and the mapping-cone description of the third term. This proves (6) and completes the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: The zero complex is covered by the first clause of the minimal-model construction in step 3.1, where vanishing of the induced differential in every degree declares the complex minimal; the empty direct sums of steps 5.1 and 6.1 are the zero object and carry the conventional vanishing character.

Zero differentials define minimality in step 3.1, and the deletion of a contractible two-term summand in step 3.1 removes exactly the blocks on which the reduced differential vanishes; step 8.1 tests triangles whose characters vanish in the same way.

The multiplicity-one case is computed first: steps 6.1 and 7.1 evaluate the graded Hom space for a single copy of each indecomposable before extending to arbitrary multiplicities, and the isomorphisms of the minimal-model statement rely only on that local case.

Non-minimal, that is degenerate, complexes are not excluded but reduced: step 3.1 splits off a contractible two-term summand across an invertible block, and step 4.1 shows any two minimal models are isomorphic, so the construction removes precisely the null-homotopic part.

Boundedness is used at both grading ends: the minimal-model iteration of step 3.1 terminates because the complex has finitely many nonzero terms, and step 4.1 applies degreewise to bounded complexes, so no end of the complex is left untreated.

Choice-free: minimal models are produced by finitely many Gaussian eliminations in steps 3.1 and 4.1, each performed on one explicitly invertible differential block, with no selection from an infinite family.

boundaries.reason: The six clauses assert semisimplicity of the quotient, existence and uniqueness of minimal models and intrinsicness of the cuts; none is formulated as one direction of a biconditional.
No equivalence is claimed in the statement, so there is no reverse direction to discharge.

citations.quote:
**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad
   \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad
   \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,
the simple reflections $s_i$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and recall that $R$ is
a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule and that shifts are defined as in
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]. For $1\le i\le n-1$ put
$$B_i:=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1),$$
the balanced tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]])
of the $(R,R^{s_i})$-bimodule $R$ with the $(R^{s_i},R)$-bimodule $R$, equipped
with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.

**The two outer actions.** The left $R$-action is $r'(r\otimes r'')=r'r\otimes r''$
and the right $R$-action is $(r\otimes r'')r'=r\otimes r''r'$; both descend to
the balanced tensor product, they commute, they are homogeneous of degree $0$,
and they satisfy $R$-linearity on the relevant side, so $B_i$ is a graded
$(R,R)$-bimodule over $R^{s_i}$-balanced tensors. Explicitly, the $(R,R)$-bimodule
$B_i$ is generated by the two elements $1\otimes1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$, which
are homogeneous of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ respectively: $\alpha_i$ is a
degree-$2$ element of $R$ and the external shift moves degrees by $-1$.

**Elementary structure.** Since $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q$, we have the
decomposition $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ (the averaging idempotent
$\tfrac12(1+s_i)$ and its complement), so as a graded left $R$-module and again
as a graded right $R$-module
$$B_i\cong R(-1)\oplus R(1),$$
and $B_i$ is finite free of rank two on each side. The Demazure operator
$\partial_i$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]] is
$R^{s_i}$-linear and surjective onto $R^{s_i}$, and
$\partial_i(\alpha_i h)=2h$ for $h\in R^{s_i}$,
a fact used when the exact sequences of $B_i$ are displayed later on this page.

**Small $n$.** For $n=0$ or $n=1$ there are no simple reflections and no
$B_i$. The only word is the empty word, with bimodule $R$; the additive graded
Bott–Samelson category contains all finite direct sums of shifts of $R$ and
all degree-zero bimodule maps between them.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Equivalently, $w\rho$ is positive on $\alpha_i^\vee$ exactly when $s_iw$ is
longer than $w$, so the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The bottom degree of $B_x^R$ is $-\ell(x)$ and its
top degree is $+\ell(x)$; on a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here
$d=\ell(x)$; $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on
$\overline{B_x^R}$, and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the Hodge-Riemann relations
with the standard sign for this normalized form. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ for the restriction of the
intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

derivations.claim: **Non-dominance.** The reflection $s$ exchanges $x_1$ and $x_2$, so $\rho'=x_1+x_2$ is $s$-invariant and $\rho'(\alpha^\vee)=(x_1+x_2,x_1-x_2)=1-1=0$ in the standard form of the coordinate normalization; in particular $\rho'$ is not strictly dominant.

**The left action of $\rho'$ equals its right action.** Since $\rho'\in S^{s}$, the balanced tensor relation gives $\rho'\otimes1=1\otimes\rho'$ in $B_s$; hence for every $b\in B_s$ the left multiplication $\rho'\cdot b$ equals the right multiplication $b\cdot\rho'$: indeed both actions are $S$-linear and the identity holds on the two basis elements $c_{\mathrm{id}}$ (where $\rho'\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=\rho'\otimes1=1\otimes\rho'=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot\rho'$) and $c_s$ (where both equal $c_s\rho'$ by [F1]).

**The operator vanishes on the reduced module.** By step 2.1, $\rho'\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot\rho'=1\otimes\rho'$ lies in $B_sS_+$, since it is the right product of $c_{\mathrm{id}}=1\otimes1$ with $\rho'\in S_+$; by [F2] its class in $\overline{B_s}$ is zero, so $\rho'\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=0$. Similarly $\rho'\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot\rho'=c_s\rho'$ lies in $B_sS_+$ and reduces to zero. Since $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ and $\overline{c_s}$ span $\overline{B_s}$, the induced operator $L=\rho'\cdot(-)$ is the zero endomorphism of $\overline{B_s}$.

**Failure of hard Lefschetz.** The reduced module has $\dim(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_s})^{1}=1$ with bases $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ and $\overline{c_s}$. The degree-one Lefschetz map $L:(\overline{B_s})^{-1}\to(\overline{B_s})^{1}$ is zero by step 3.1, hence not an isomorphism, and hard Lefschetz fails for $L$ in the sense of [F3]. The bottom Lefschetz form $\langle-,L(-)\rangle$ is likewise identically zero, so the Hodge-Riemann relations with any nonzero sign also fail.

**The general degree-two case.** Let $\rho''=ax_1+bx_2$ satisfy $\rho''(\alpha^\vee)=a-b=0$; then $a=b$ and $\rho''=a\rho'$ is a scalar multiple of $\rho'$. If $a=0$ the operator is trivially zero; if $a\ne0$ the same computation as in steps 2.1-4.1 applies because invariance and positivity of degree are unaffected by the scalar. Hence every degree-two element with vanishing evaluation on $\alpha_s^\vee$ yields the zero operator on the reduced rank-one module and fails hard Lefschetz. This proves the claimed failure and shows that strict dominance is a necessary hypothesis; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The item is a single explicit rank-one computation with fixed two-dimensional module and fixed basis; no family, indexed aggregate or empty construction occurs in the refuted statement.

boundaries.evidence: The zero operator is the mechanism of the failure: step 3.1 proves the chosen element acts as zero on the reduced module, and step 5.1 covers the scalar case in which the degree-two element is itself zero, where the same failure is trivial.
The rank-one reduced module has one-dimensional graded pieces, computed in step 4.1, and that is exactly the situation in which the Lefschetz map is required to be an isomorphism and is not.

The counterexample is itself the degenerate boundary case: the element is invariant with vanishing coroot evaluation, the failure of strict dominance, and step 5.1 shows every degree-two element with vanishing evaluation on the coroot shares the failure.

The two grading endpoints are where the failure is detected: step 4.1 computes the Lefschetz map from the one-dimensional bottom degree to the one-dimensional top degree and shows it is the zero map rather than an isomorphism.
Choice-free: every step from 1.1 to 5.1 is a computation in a fixed two-dimensional real vector space with explicit bases.

boundaries.reason: The statement refuted is a failure assertion together with a necessity conclusion; no biconditional is claimed, so there is no forward direction.
No converse direction exists: the item proves that strict dominance cannot be dropped, not that two conditions are equivalent.

citations.quote:
Let $H$ have a graded non-degenerate symmetric form and a symmetric degree-two operator $L$.

(a) If hL holds then $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$; more precisely, in each degree $-i$ one has $H^{-i}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$.

(b) In each degree $-i$, the decomposition of (a) is orthogonal for the Lefschetz form $\langle a,L^ib\rangle$.

(c) All Lefschetz forms on $H^{-i}$ are non-degenerate exactly when hL holds.

(d) If $H$ has one parity and lowest degree $-d$, standard HR is equivalent to hL together with the signature formula $\operatorname{sig}\bigl(\langle-,L^i-\rangle|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}\dim P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ for every $i\ge0$ (zero spaces omitted).

(e) An $L$-stable graded subspace $V\subseteq H$ with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$ inherits hL; if $H$ satisfies HR then the restricted form on $V$ is non-degenerate and $V$ inherits the ambient primitive signs, and its standard global sign agrees with that of $H$ when their lowest degrees coincide.

Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space is congruent to exactly one normal form

$$\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r),\qquad p+q+r=\dim V.$$

Equivalently, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries are independent of the diagonalizing basis.

Let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and write $q(v):=B(v,v)$. The form is **positive definite** when $q(v)>0$ for every $v\ne0$, and **negative definite** when $q(v)<0$ for every $v\ne0$. The same terminology applies to the associated quadratic form.

Suppose a basis gives a diagonal matrix with $p$ positive diagonal entries, $q$ negative diagonal entries, and $r$ zero entries. Its **inertia** is the triple $(p,q,r)$, its **rank** is $p+q$, and its **signature** is $p-q$. Sylvester's law of inertia proves that this triple is independent of the diagonalizing basis, and therefore justifies the notation.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

derivations.claim: **The family lemma (1).** Fix $i\ge0$ and consider the family of symmetric forms $(a,b)\mapsto\langle a,L_t^ib\rangle$ on the fixed space $H^{-i}$. For each $t$ it is non-degenerate, because hL makes $L_t^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ an isomorphism and the ambient form pairs $H^i$ perfectly with $H^{-i}$; and it depends continuously on $t$ because $L_t$ does. By [F2] its signature is locally constant in $t$ on the connected interval $[a,b]$, hence constant. At $t_0$ the primitive decomposition of $L_{t_0}$ is orthogonal for this form with definite primitive blocks, so the signature at every $t$ equals the $t_0$ signature. Moreover the primitive dimensions are the same for every $t$: $\dim P_{L_t}^{-i}=\dim H^{-i}-\dim H^{-i-2}$ for all $t$, by the string decomposition of [F1] applied to each $L_t$. Descending induction on $i$ from the top degree in the signature formula of [F1] now shows that the primitive Lefschetz forms of $L_t$ have the $t_0$-signs for every $t$: at the top nonzero degree the signature of $H^{-i}$ is the signature of the primitive form, and inductively subtract the contributions of the already-determined higher primitive spaces, whose dimensions do not depend on $t$. Since non-degenerate forms on the primitive spaces have signature $\pm\dim$, this gives the standard-sign definiteness for every $t$. In the application $L_\zeta=L_0+\zeta M$ with $M$ the middle-position operator is polynomial in $\zeta$, hence continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and on every compact subinterval. This proves (1).

**The weak-Lefschetz substitute, injectivity (2).** For $i=0$ the map $L^0$ is the identity. Let $i\ge1$ and $0
e a\in V^{-i}$; then $-i\le-1$, so $\varphi(a)
e0$ by (a). If $L^i\varphi(a)
e0$, then $L^i a
e0$ because $L^i\varphi(a)=\varphi(L^i a)$ (the map is $R[L]$-linear). Otherwise $L^i\varphi(a)=0$, so $\varphi(a)$ is a nonzero primitive vector in $W^{-i+1}$; the HR relations of $W$ give that the Lefschetz value $(\varphi(a),\varphi(a))_L^{-i+1}=\langle\varphi(a),L^{i-1}\varphi(a)angle_W$ is definite nonzero. By (b) this equals $\langle a,L^iaangle_V$; in particular $L^ia
e0$. Hence $L^i$ is injective in both cases. If moreover $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, injectivity plus equality of finite dimensions makes each $L^i:V^{-i}	o V^i$ an isomorphism, which is hL on $V$. This proves (2).

**Sign bookkeeping (3).** In the situation of step 2.1 with $i=\ell+1$, one has $-i+1=-\ell$, the lowest degree of $W$, and the computation of step 2.1 shows that the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is definite with the sign of the primitive form of $W$ in degree $-\ell$, which is the sign prescribed by the standard-sign HR of $W$; the global factor of the HR statement of $V$, if any, is thereby fixed, and $V$ has the standard sign exactly when $W$ does. This proves (3).

**The degenerate shifted case (4).** Put $Q_L^{-d-i}:=\ker(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-d-i}})\subseteq H^{-d-i}$ for $i\ge0$, and $Q^{-d-i}_L:=0$ for $i<0$. The hypothesis that $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ gives the shifted primitive decomposition $H^m=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^jQ_L^{m-2j}$ by the same string argument as the primitive decomposition of [F1], with the centering shifted by $d$. Fix $m\le0$, $x\in Q^{m-2j}_L$, $y\in Q^{m-2k}_L$ with $j\ge k\ge0$; then $(L^jx,L^ky)_L^m=\langle x,L^{j+k-m}y\rangle$. Now $y\in Q^{m-2k}_L=\ker(L^{i+1})$ with $-d-i=m-2k$, i.e. $i=2k-m-d$, so $y$ is killed by $L^{2k-m-d+1}$; and $j+k-m\ge 2k-m-d+1$ because $j\ge k\ge k-d+1$ as $d>0$. Hence the pairing vanishes for arbitrary primitive vectors and arbitrary blocks, so the Lefschetz form on $H^{-m}$ is identically zero. This proves (4).

**The stable-subspace lemma (5).** Let $V\subseteq H$ be $L$-stable with symmetric dimensions. Since $L^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ is injective, its restriction to $V^{-i}$ is injective, and the dimension equality makes it an isomorphism onto $V^i$; so $V$ satisfies hL. The primitive subspace of $V$ is $P_V^{-i}=V^{-i}\cap P_L^{-i}$, because the kernel of $L^{i+1}$ on $V^{-i}$ is the intersection of $V^{-i}$ with the kernel on $H^{-i}$; the restricted Lefschetz form on $P_V^{-i}$ is the restriction of the ambient definite primitive form, hence definite with the ambient sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$. By the primitive decomposition applied inside $V$ (step 2.1 of [[lem-hard-lefschetz-implies-primitive-decomposition]] gives it from hL on $V$), the restricted form on $V$ is an orthogonal sum of definite blocks, hence non-degenerate, and its signs are the ambient signs; if the lowest nonzero degree of $V$ is $-d$, the ambient standard sign is also the standard sign of $V$. This proves (5) and completes the lemma; no choice principle is used.

citations.quote: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

derivations.claim: **A split counit.** Put $U:=M\otimes_{S^s}S$, so that $MB_s=M\otimes_S(S\otimes_{S^s}S(1))=U(1)$. The multiplication counit $c:U\to M$, $c(b\otimes r):=br$, is a degree-zero left $S$-linear map and is surjective because $b\otimes1\mapsto b$. By the $S^s$-decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ the module $U$ is $M\oplus M(\alpha_s/2)$ as a right $S^s$-module, and the lowest degree of $U$ is the one-dimensional space $M^{-\ell(x)}\otimes1$; the counit restricts to the identity there and to zero on the $\alpha_s$-summand in the lowest degree. Since the lowest degree of $M$ is one-dimensional by [F1], the restriction of $c$ to the first summand is a nonzero scalar endomorphism of the line $M^{-\ell(x)}$ and is therefore invertible.

**The section and the twisted counit.** Rescaling the inclusion of the first summand by the inverse scalar of step 1.1 gives a degree-zero $S$-linear section $\sigma:M\to U$ with $c\circ\sigma=\mathrm{id}_M$; it is automatically left $S$-linear and embeds $M$ as a direct summand of $U$. Define the twisted counit $c_s:U\to M_s$ by $c_s(b\otimes r):=b\,s(r)$. It is balanced over $S^s$, left $S$-linear, and right $S$-semilinear in the sense $c_s(u r)=c_s(u)\,s(r)$; in particular the composite $t:=c_s\circ\sigma:M\to M$ is a degree-zero, left $S$-linear, right-$s$-semilinear endomorphism. On the lowest degree $\sigma(b)=b\otimes1$ for $b$ in the bottom line, so $t(b)=b\,s(1)=b$ there.

**The involution property of $t$.** Since $t$ is right-$s$-semilinear and degree zero, $t^2$ is an ordinary degree-zero $S$-bimodule endomorphism of $M$, hence a scalar by $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$; its scalar is $1$ because $t^2$ acts as the identity on the one-dimensional bottom degree by step 2.1. Hence $t^2=\mathrm{id}_M$.

**The descent isomorphism.** For $u\in U$ one has $c_s(u)-c(u)\in M\alpha_s$, because $s(r)-r\in\alpha_s S$ for every $r\in S$; consequently $t(m)-m\in M\alpha_s$ for every $m\in M$. Define $N:=\{m\in M: t(m)=m\}$. Every $m$ splits as $m=\tfrac12(m+t(m))+\tfrac12(m-t(m))$ into an invariant and an anti-invariant part, and an anti-invariant $m$ (that is, $t(m)=-m$) lies in $M\alpha_s$, say $m=n\alpha_s$; since right multiplication by $\alpha_s$ is injective by [F2] and $t(m)=-m$ with $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ gives $t(n\alpha_s)=t(n)s(\alpha_s)=-t(n)\alpha_s$ and hence $t(n)=n$, we get $n\in N$ and the anti-invariant part of $m$ is $N\alpha_s$. Therefore $M=N\oplus N\alpha_s$ as $(S,S^s)$-bimodules, and the multiplication map induces an isomorphism $N\otimes_{S^s}S\to M$; this proves the descent isomorphism.

**The matrix of $L_\zeta$.** Fix the isomorphism $MB_s=U(1)\cong(M\oplus M(-2))(1)=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$ induced by $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$, with structure maps $\iota_1,\iota_2,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of [F2] satisfying $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$. In this basis, middle multiplication by $\rho$ has entries $\pi_1(\rho)$, $\pi_1(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and $\partial_s(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, and the operators of multiplication by $\rho$ on the two outer factors contribute the same diagonal $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$. All entries except the off-diagonal $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ have positive polynomial degree in $\rho$ and vanish after the right reduction; the off-diagonal entry has the constant term $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and contributes the degree-two map $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee):M(1)\to M(-1)$; hence, after reduction, $L_\zeta$ is the displayed matrix.

**Hard Lefschetz for $\zeta>0$.** Assume $\mathrm{hL}(x)$, so the reduced module $\overline M$ is a direct sum of centered $\rho$-strings $u_0,\ldots,u_m$ with $\deg u_j=j$ and $\rho u_j=u_{j+1}$; on each string, left multiplication by $\rho$ is the standard nilpotent Jordan block. In the two-dimensional middle factor with basis $v_-,v_+$ of degrees $-1,+1$ and $e(v_-)=\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)v_+$, $e(v_+)=0$, the operator $e=L_\zeta$ on the string tensor $\bigoplus_j u_j\otimes\{v_-,v_+\}$ acts by $e^k(u_jv_-)=u_{j+k}v_-+k\,u_{j+k-1}v_+$ and $e^k(u_jv_+)=u_{j+k}v_+$ (indices out of range zero), after normalizing the nonzero scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ to $1$ by rescaling $v_+$; in centered degree $-k$ with $0\le k\le m+1$ the source basis $u_{(m+1-k)/2}v_-,\,u_{(m-1-k)/2}v_+$ and the corresponding target basis exhibit $e^k$ as a matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $1$, lower-left entry $k$, and upper-right entry $0$, which is invertible; at $k=m+1$ the map sends $u_0v_-$ to $(m+1)u_mv_+$, nonzero by the normalization $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$. The operator on each string is thus an isomorphism in every centered degree, and $L_\zeta$ on the direct sum of strings satisfies hL. Positivity of $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ uses $\zeta>0$ and strict dominance of $\rho$.

**Failure at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of step 5.1 is diagonal with respect to the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$. The bottom class $b\in\overline M^{-\ell(x)}$ sits in the first summand in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$ because $\overline M^{-\ell(x)-1}=0$; the opposite class in $M(1)$ of degree $\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality and dimension symmetry. Hence $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}$ is not injective on $\overline{MB_s}$ in the centered grading and centered hL fails at $\zeta=0$, even though the two individual shifted copies of $\overline M$ have their own strings centered at $\pm1$. Steps 1.1-5.1 prove the descent isomorphism and the matrix, step 6.1 the positive-parameter hard Lefschetz, and this step the failure at zero; no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$ is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement fixes the bimodule M and its two-term product MB_s = M(1) + M(-1); every index occurring in it is determined by that fixed pair, so there is no empty family to interpret.

boundaries.evidence: The zero parameter is one of the two regimes analysed: step 5.1 computes the matrix for general parameter, step 6.1 proves hard Lefschetz for positive parameter by rescaling, and step 7.1 exhibits the diagonal zero-parameter matrix whose bottom class fails injectivity.

The two multiplicity-one summands M(1) and M(-1) are isolated in steps 5.1 and 6.1, and the one-dimensional space spanned by the bottom class is what step 7.1 uses to detect the zero-parameter failure.

Degeneracy occurs exactly at the vanishing parameter: in step 7.1 the strict inequality defining the relevant Lefschetz map collapses when the scaling factor vanishes, and that collapse is what separates the two parameter regimes.

The internal-degree endpoints of the two summands drive the matrix computations: step 5.1 tracks the matrices of L_zeta on M(1) and M(-1), and step 7.1 evaluates the centred map at the bottom degree of the first summand.
Choice-free: the splitting of the invariant ring in step 1.1 is an explicit direct sum, the section sigma is defined by a formula in step 2.1, and the scalar t is computed in step 3.1.

boundaries.reason: The lemma displays an isomorphism, a matrix and two parameter statements; none of its clauses is an equivalence, so there is no forward direction to check.
No converse is asserted: the descent isomorphism and the positivity threshold are proved directly rather than as one half of a biconditional.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here
$d=\ell(x)$; $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on
$\overline{B_x^R}$, and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the Hodge-Riemann relations
with the standard sign for this normalized form. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ for the restriction of the
intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

Let $H$ have a graded non-degenerate symmetric form and a symmetric degree-two operator $L$.

(a) If hL holds then $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$; more precisely, in each degree $-i$ one has $H^{-i}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$.

(b) In each degree $-i$, the decomposition of (a) is orthogonal for the Lefschetz form $\langle a,L^ib\rangle$.

(c) All Lefschetz forms on $H^{-i}$ are non-degenerate exactly when hL holds.

(d) If $H$ has one parity and lowest degree $-d$, standard HR is equivalent to hL together with the signature formula $\operatorname{sig}\bigl(\langle-,L^i-\rangle|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}\dim P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ for every $i\ge0$ (zero spaces omitted).

(e) An $L$-stable graded subspace $V\subseteq H$ with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$ inherits hL; if $H$ satisfies HR then the restricted form on $V$ is non-degenerate and $V$ inherits the ambient primitive signs, and its standard global sign agrees with that of $H$ when their lowest degrees coincide.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
