Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d>0$. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the complex is $F_e=S$, $m=0$, and for $j=0$ the space $^0F_e(0)=S$ satisfies hL and HR trivially: its lowest degree is $0$, the primitive subspace $P^0=\mathbb R$ carries the positive definite form $\langle1,1\rangle>0$, and $0\equiv-m+j\pmod4$, so the global sign is the standard one; there are no $j\ge1$ terms.

**Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$ and assume the statement for every $y<x$. Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$, $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$ and $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$ and $F_x$ is a summand of $F_yF_s$; fix an embedding $F_y\subseteq^{\oplus}F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_{m-1}}$ witnessing the induction hypothesis and use it to embed $F_x\subseteq^{\oplus}F_yF_s\subset F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$. For every $j$ this gives the embedding chain of [F1], $^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}{}^jF_yB_s(-j)\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$, and the induction hypothesis applies to ${}^jF_y(-j)$ and to ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ with the global signs indexed by $y$; by [F2] the $j$-th term of $F_x$ is linear.

**The decomposition of the middle term and orthogonality.** Under $\mathrm S(\le x)$ the comparison lemma gives a decomposition of the multiplicity space, so ${}^jF_y(-j)=\bigoplus_{z}V_z\otimes_\mathbb RB_z$ with degree-zero multiplicity spaces $V_z$; define $B^\uparrow=\bigoplus_{zs>z}V_z\otimes B_z$ and $B^\downarrow=\bigoplus_{zs<z}V_z\otimes B_z$, so that ${}^jF_y(-j)=B^\uparrow\oplus B^\downarrow$. The decomposition is orthogonal for the induced form because $\operatorname{Hom}(B^\uparrow,D B^\downarrow)=\operatorname{Hom}(B^\downarrow,DB^\uparrow)=0$ for non-isomorphic indecomposables under $\mathrm S$; character calculations give that $B^\uparrow B_s$ is perverse and that $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(-1)\oplus B^\downarrow(1)$.

**The shifted descent piece does not contribute.** In the decomposition $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(1)\oplus B^\downarrow(-1)$ the restriction of the Lefschetz form to $B^\downarrow(1)$ is identically zero: left multiplication by $\rho$ satisfies hL on $B^\downarrow$ (each summand $B_z$ with $zs<z$ satisfies the induction hypothesis and hence HR, and the lowest degree shifts by one under tensoring), so [F5] applies to the shifted piece with $d>0$. Moreover the projection of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ to $B^\downarrow B_s$ lands entirely in $B^\downarrow(1)$: ${}^jF_x(-j)$ lives in perverse degree $0$ by the linearity theorem, and Hom-vanishing between perverse degrees $0$ and $-1$ forces the projection to the $B^\downarrow(-1)$-part to vanish. Hence the image of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ in $B^\downarrow B_s$ contributes nothing to the Lefschetz form.

**The isometry into the surviving target.** By step 4.1 the projection of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ to the remaining factors is an isometry for the Lefschetz forms: the inclusion ${}^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}{}^jF_yB_s(-j)\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ restricts to a $\rho$-equivariant map $\jmath$ into $B^\uparrow B_s\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ with $\langle b,L_0b'\rangle=\langle\jmath(b),\jmath(b')\rangle$ for all $b,b'$. The map $\jmath$ is injective: applying the quotient functor $q$ to the split inclusion ${}^jF_x\hookrightarrow{}^j(F_yF_s)$ gives a split injection, while a nonzero map ${}^jF_x(-j)\to B^\downarrow(1)$ would be a map between perverse degrees $0$ and $-1$ and hence vanishes after $q$; therefore the induced map to the complement of $B^\downarrow(1)$ is a split injection after $q$ and so is injective.

**The codomain satisfies the relations with the global sign.** The two orthogonal summands of the codomain are handled as follows. The summand ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ satisfies HR with the global sign of the induction hypothesis for $y$ and $j-1$, namely positivity on primitive degrees congruent to $-\ell(y)+(j-1)=-m+1+j-1=-m+j\pmod4$, which is the required global sign for $x,j$. The summand $B^\uparrow B_s$ satisfies HR by the tensoring lemma [F3]: $B^\uparrow$ is a self-dual direct sum of normalized $B_z$ with $zs>z$, each satisfying $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)$ by hypothesis and hence hL and HR with the standard sign; step 3.1 shows it is even or odd with the induced sign, so $B^\uparrow B_s$ satisfies HR with the global sign obtained by raising the degree by one, i.e. positivity on degrees congruent to $(-\ell(y)+j)-1=-m+j\pmod4$. Since the two summands are orthogonal and carry the same global sign, the codomain satisfies HR with the global sign fixed by $-m+j$.

**The source inherits the relations.** The map $\jmath$ of step 5.1 identifies ${}^jF_x(-j)$ isometrically with a $\rho$-stable graded subspace of a space satisfying hL and HR, and ${}^jF_x(-j)$ has symmetric Betti numbers by [F1]; by the stable-subspace lemma [F4] the space ${}^jF_x(-j)$ inherits hL and HR from the codomain, and the signature of the restricted Lefschetz form on its primitive subspaces is the one induced by the ambient normalization, which is the global sign fixed by $-m+j$. This holds for every $j$ and every tuple $\lambda$ of strictly positive rescalings, since the rescaling preserves definiteness and its sign; hence $F_x$ satisfies the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations as stated.

boundaries.evidence: The empty word is the base of the induction in step 1.1: the complex is the unit concentrated in degree zero, its single summand satisfies the relations trivially, and the existence of the embedding as a direct summand is the identity statement.

The degree-zero summand is the top term of the induction: step 2.1 keeps it as the induction hypothesis for the shorter element, and step 4.1 shows the shifted descent piece contributes nothing to the surviving target.

Unit multiplicity is tracked explicitly: step 3.1 decomposes the fixed degree piece into multiplicity spaces attached to the summands, and step 6.1 handles the single top summand separately from the lower ones.

Degenerate summands are isolated rather than assumed absent: step 4.1 identifies the shifted descent piece whose Lefschetz form vanishes identically and shows it is orthogonal to the surviving summands, so the defect cannot propagate.
The lowest degree of each piece is the anchor of the statement: the conventions fix the bottom degree, and steps 2.1 and 5.1 verify the isometry and the signs beginning at that degree.
Choice-free: the tuples of positive rescaling factors are fixed data of the statement, and the induction of steps 2.1 through 7.1 ranges over finitely many summands.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts existence of an embedding satisfying a list of positivity conditions; it contains no biconditional and thus no forward direction.
No converse obligation arises: the statement does not claim that the Hodge-Riemann signs characterize the minimal complex.

Let $M=B_x^R$ over $S$ and let $s$ be a right descent, $xs<x$. Assume $\mathrm{S}(x)$. Then there is a graded $(S,S^s)$-bimodule $N$ and an isomorphism $M\cong N\otimes_{S^s}S$. Consequently $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$; choosing the decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ in the middle tensor factor, the reduced operator $L_\zeta$ has, with respect to the resulting identification $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, the matrix
$$L_\zeta=\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix},$$
where the scalar off-diagonal entry is a degree-two map $M(1)\to M(-1)$. The construction requires no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$. If $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ also holds and $\zeta>0$, this matrix satisfies centered hard Lefschetz; at $\zeta=0$ it fails centered hard Lefschetz.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

(1) **Right-module retraction.** For every $x$ and every reduced expression of $x$, the minimal Rouquier complex $F_x$ is homotopy equivalent, as a complex of graded right $S$-modules, to the single right module $S(-\ell(x))$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$. Consequently the right reduction has $H^0(\overline{F_x})\cong\mathbb R(-\ell(x))$, one copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $\ell(x)$, and $H^j(\overline{F_x})=0$ for $j\ne0$.

(2) **Injectivity criterion.** Let $C$ be a bounded below complex of graded free right $S$-modules with $C^{-1}=0$ whose right reduction satisfies $H^{-1}(\overline C)=0$ and whose $H^0(\overline C)$ is concentrated in a single internal degree $d$. Then the reduced first differential $\overline{d^0}:\overline{C^0}\to\overline{C^1}$ is injective in every internal degree $\ne d$; in particular it is injective in internal degrees $\le d-1$. The conclusion is unchanged if $C$ is replaced by a homotopy-equivalent complex $C'$ with $C'^{-1}=0$ obtained by cancelling contractible two-term summands whose source lies in a positive cohomological degree, in particular the contractible shifted-descent summands occurring in the zero-parameter hard-Lefschetz theorem.

(3) **Application to the ascent differential.** Let $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$. Then the first differential of the complex $F_xF_s$, whose source is $B_x^RB_s^R$ and whose target is $^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x^R(1)$, has reduced form injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$. The complex $F_xF_s$ need not itself be minimal, and no minimality is used in the conclusion.

(4) **Separation of inputs.** The form compatibility $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle=\langle\varphi b,\varphi b'\rangle_\gamma$ and the operator commutation $\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\varphi(b)$ used in the hard-Lefschetz proof are independent additional inputs supplied by the deleted-word factorization and the induced forms; in the zero-parameter descent case the form on the shifted descent piece vanishes and the hard-Lefschetz argument must separate the kernel of $d_3$ rather than apply the criterion of (2) to the whole target.

(1) **Family lemma.** Let $L_t$, $t\in[a,b]$, be a continuous family of symmetric degree-two operators on $H$, each satisfying hL, and suppose $L_{t_0}$ satisfies HR with the standard sign for one $t_0\in[a,b]$. Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d>0$. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.

Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(y,s)$ for every $y<x$ and simple $s$ with $ys>y$. Fix a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$. Then $F_x$ satisfies the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations in the following sense: there exists an embedding as a direct summand $F_x\subseteq^{\oplus}F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ such that for every tuple $\lambda=(\lambda_{x'})_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}$ of strictly positive real numbers and every $j\ge0$, the space $^jF_x(-j)$ embedded in $\bigoplus_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}\mathrm{BS}(x')$ carries the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with respect to the rescaled form $\langle-,-\rangle_\lambda$ and the Lefschetz operator given by left multiplication by $\rho$, with the global sign fixed so that the Lefschetz form is positive definite on the primitive subspaces in degrees congruent to $-m+j\pmod4$. Here $\pi(x,j)$ is the set of subexpressions of $\underline x$ obtained by deleting $j$ letters and $^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}\bigoplus_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}\mathrm{BS}(x')$ is the canonical summand inclusion of [F1]. The conclusion is independent of the choice of the reduced expression, since a different reduced expression changes the embedding but not the resulting intersection forms up to positive scalar.

Fix $\zeta\ge0$ and a self-dual Soergel bimodule $B=\bigoplus_zB_z^{R,m_z}$ such that $m_z\ne0$ implies $\mathrm{S}(z)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)_\zeta$; if $\zeta=0$ assume in addition that $m_z=0$ whenever $zs<z$. Assume $B$ is even or odd, carries an invariant non-degenerate form and satisfies HR with the standard sign with respect to left multiplication by $\rho$. Then $BB_s$ satisfies HR with the standard sign with respect to $L_\zeta$ and the induced form. More precisely, if the lowest degree of $B$ is $-d$, then the restriction of its form to a $B_z$ summand is $(-1)^{(d-\ell(z))/2}$ times a positive multiple of the normalized form on $B_z$. Tensoring gives the primitive sign $(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}$ on degree $-i$ of $BB_s$, whose lowest degree is $-d-1$.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad
\tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad
\tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

derivations.claim: **Case (1), positive parameter.** Assume $xs<x$, $\mathrm S(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(x)$. By [F1] the reduced operator is the matrix with diagonal blocks $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $B_x(1)$ and $B_x(-1)$ and lower off-diagonal block $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$, a scalar multiple of the identity; since $\rho\cdot(-)$ satisfies hL on $B_x$, the $\rho$-action completes to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)$-action and, after rescaling by $\zeta\ne0$, the matrix describes the action of the raising operator on the tensor product of $B_x$ with the two-dimensional standard representation; hence its powers are isomorphisms in the centered degrees and $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds, which is case (1).

**Case (2), setting and form identity.** Assume $\zeta>0$, $xs>x$, $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$. By [F2] the scalars $\gamma_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ are strictly positive and $\gamma_{m+1}=(x^{-1}\rho)(\alpha_s^\vee)+\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$, and with $\varphi:M\to{}^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x(1)$ the first differential of $F_xF_s$ one has $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle_{\overline M}=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle_\gamma$ for all $b,b'\in M$; by [F3] the reduced $\varphi$ is injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$.

**Failure at $\zeta=0$ for a descent.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of [F1] is diagonal with both diagonal blocks the Lefschetz operator of $B_x$; the bottom class $b$ of $B_x(1)$ lies in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$, so the centered Lefschetz map of degree $-\ell(x)-1$ fails to be injective; the opposite total degree $+\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality of $B_xB_s$, so the failure is genuine and not a vanishing of both sides. This is the failure statement of the theorem.

**The operator commutes with $\varphi$.** Writing $\varphi=(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1$ into ${}^1F_xB_s(-1)$ and $d_2$ into $B_x(1)$, the deleted-word factorization of [F2] shows that $d_1$ commutes with $L_\zeta$ and that $d_2(L_\zeta b)=\rho\cdot d_2(b)+d_2(b)\cdot\zeta\rho$; hence, with respect to the operator $L$ equal to $L_\zeta$ on the first summand and $\rho\cdot(-)$ on the second, one has $\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\varphi(b)$ for all $b\in M$.

**The target satisfies HR.** Consider the graded space $W:={}^1F_x(-1)B_s\oplus B_x$ with the operator $L$ of step 2.2 and the form $\langle-,-\rangle_\gamma$. The two summands are orthogonal for the induced form, $B_x$ satisfies hL and HR by $\mathrm{HR}(x)$, and ${}^1F_x(-1)B_s$ satisfies hL and HR with the standard sign: its summands $B_z$ with $z<x$ satisfy $\mathrm S(z)$ and, for those with $zs>z$, the hypothesis $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)_\zeta$ (which $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ supplies), so the tensoring lemma [F6] applies to ${}^1F_x(-1)=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z$ with the positivity of the rescalings; the induced signs of ${}^1F_x(-1)$ furnished by [F5] match the standard sign. Hence $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign, and the map $\varphi$ sends $M$ into $W(1)$ because ${}^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x(1)={}^1F_x(-1)B_s(1)\oplus B_x(1)=W(1)$.

**Case (2) concluded.** Apply the weak-Lefschetz substitute [F4] to $\varphi:M\to W(1)$: its three hypotheses hold by steps 1.2, 2.2 and 3.1 (injectivity in degrees $\le\ell(x)$ contains injectivity in degrees $\le-1$, the form identity is the one of [F2], and $W$ satisfies HR by step 3.1). Hence $L_\zeta^k:M^{-k}\to M^k$ is injective for all $k\ge0$; since $M$ is self-dual and has symmetric Betti numbers, equal dimensions give isomorphisms, which is $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ and proves case (2).

**Case (3), the separated differential.** Assume $\zeta=0$, $xs>x$, $\mathrm S(\le x)$, the ascent HR hypothesis for lower elements, $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(z)$ for all $z<xs$. Use the same positive scalars $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{m+1}$ with $\zeta=0$ and the same form identity as in [F2] with $\varphi$ the first differential of $F_xF_s$. Decompose ${}^1F_x(-1)=B^\uparrow\oplus B^\downarrow$ orthogonally according to $zs>z$ and $zs<z$ as in step 3.1; by [F7] the complex $F_xF_s$ lies in $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and the restriction of its second differential to $\tau_{\le-2}(B^\downarrow B_s(1))$ is a split injection, so cancelling that contractible summand leaves a homotopy-equivalent complex with first differential $d=(d_1,d_2,d_3):B_xB_s\to B_x(1)\oplus B^\uparrow B_s(1)\oplus B^\downarrow$, all components commuting with left multiplication by $\rho$, and $d$ injective in degrees $\le\ell(x)$ by [F3].

**Conclusion and caveats.** Steps 1.1-1.2 treat the descent cases, step 4.1 case (2) and step 5.1 case (3); no step assumes HR for the unseparated zero-parameter descent target, and no step invokes any singular-category descent theorem or any statement beyond the suppliers listed. This proves the three-case theorem and the failure statement.

boundaries.reason: The theorem fixes the ascent or descent pair and the bimodule built from it; the three listed cases are exhaustive and the statement contains no empty family or empty summation needing interpretation.

boundaries.evidence: The zero parameter is an entire case of the theorem: step 2.1 exhibits the failure at vanishing parameter in the descent situation, while steps 4.2 and 5.1 prove the ascent case there by separating the kernel of the third differential component.
The multiplicity-one summands B_x(1) and B_x(-1) of the descent decomposition, and the single top summand B_x of the target constructed in step 3.1, are the unit-multiplicity pieces the proof tracks.

The degenerate zero-parameter descent case is genuinely excluded from hard Lefschetz and is displayed as the failure clause of step 2.1, while the positive-parameter descent case is recovered in step 1.1 by an explicit rescaling.
The parameter endpoints are separated by the case list, and the grading endpoints enter through steps 2.1 and 5.1, which evaluate the bottom class and its powers up to the extreme degree.
Choice-free: the complexes and forms are fixed by the suppliers, and the only rescaling in step 1.1 is by the explicit positive real parameter.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a three-case implication list together with a failure statement; it asserts no equivalence, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse is claimed: the hypotheses are sufficient conditions for hard Lefschetz in each case, not a characterization.

citations.quote:
Fix $x,s$ with $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm{S}(y)$ for every $y<xs$. Put $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and write the Kazhdan-Lusztig multiplication formula $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}\mu_y\underline H_y$ with integer constants $\mu_y$. For each $y<xs$ let $E_y=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ carry the local intersection form of [[def-local-intersection-form-for-a-soergel-summand]]. Then:

(1) $\dim_{\mathbb R}E_y=\mu_y$, while the full graded Hom module has graded rank $\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_s\rangle$, generally not $\mu_y$;

(2) the following are equivalent: $\mathrm{S}(xs)$; non-degeneracy of every local intersection form on $E_y$, $y<xs$; perfection of every degree-zero composition pairing $E_y\times\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)\to\operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R$; and equality of the actual multiplicity $a_y$ of $B_y^R$ in $M$ with $\mu_y$ for every $y<xs$.

The unconditional top summand is $B_{xs}$ with multiplicity one, and under $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ all remaining summands are unshifted $B_y^R$. No positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials or conjecture at $xs$ is assumed.

The hard Lefschetz theorem for $L_\zeta$ on $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ holds in the following three cases.

(1) $\zeta>0$ and $xs<x$: under $\mathrm S(x)$, $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ implies $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$. The $\mathrm{hL}(x)$-only descent implication, with the same matrix and without an assumed $\mathrm S(x)$, is retained as an after-induction consequence in the character theorem, where $\mathrm S(x)$ has already been proved.

(2) $\zeta>0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds.

(3) $\zeta=0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(z)$ for all $z<xs$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$ holds.

In the remaining case $\zeta=0$ and $xs<x$, centered hard Lefschetz fails: in the decomposition $B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ the operator $L_0$ is diagonal, the bottom vector of the first summand lies in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and its $(\ell(x)+1)$-st $\rho$-power is zero, while the opposite total degree is nonzero by self-duality; the two copies have Lefschetz strings centered at $-1$ and $+1$ rather than at zero.

Let $B$ be a Soergel bimodule satisfying hL and HR with the standard sign. Then for $\zeta\gg0$ the induced operator $L_\zeta$ on $BB_s$ satisfies hL and HR with the standard sign (Theorem 5.1).

The proof contains the following **signature comparison** (Lemma 5.2): if $V,W$ are finite-dimensional graded spaces with graded non-degenerate forms and Lefschetz operators satisfying hL, $W$ is even or odd, $\dim V=(v+v^{-1})\dim W$, and $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign, then $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign if and only if for all $i\ge0$ the signature of the Lefschetz form on the primitive subspace $P_W^{-i+1}$ equals the signature of the Lefschetz form on all of $V^{-i}$.

Consequently (Corollary 5.3): if $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ holds and $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for every $\zeta\ge0$, then $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for every $\zeta\ge0$; more generally, if $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for a single $\zeta_0\ge0$, then $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$. In the signature comparison use the convention $P_W^1=0$; no positive-degree primitive space is introduced.

(1) **Family lemma.** Let $L_t$, $t\in[a,b]$, be a continuous family of symmetric degree-two operators on $H$, each satisfying hL, and suppose $L_{t_0}$ satisfies HR with the standard sign for one $t_0\in[a,b]$. Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d>0$. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.

Let $xs>x$. The normalized indecomposable $B_{xs}^R$ occurs as a bimodule summand of $B_x^RB_s^R$.

(a) If $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$ holds, then $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$ holds.

(b) If $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(y)$ for every $y<xs$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$.

(c) If $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ holds, then the restriction to the chosen $B_{xs}^R$ summand satisfies the Hodge-Riemann relations for its induced form; once $\mathrm{S}(xs)$ has been established, positive comparison of invariant forms gives $\mathrm{HR}(xs)$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(xs)$ with the standard sign.

(d) More generally an $L_0$-stable graded subspace with symmetric Betti numbers inherits HR with the ambient signs, and an $L_0$-stable graded direct summand inherits hL. These conclusions apply to a positive deformation only if the chosen subspace, and for the direct-sum argument its complement, are preserved by that operator; they make no identification of the restricted positive operator with left multiplication by $\rho$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $B_s=R\otimes_{R^s}R(1)$, so that
$B_s=R\otimes_{R^s}R\{-1\}$ in the internal shift. Then there is an isomorphism
of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$B_s\otimes_RB_s\;\cong\;B_s(1)\oplus B_s(-1),$$
that is $B_s\otimes_RB_s\cong B_s\{-1\}\oplus B_s\{1\}$; the two summands are
the idempotent images of the summands $R\otimes_{R^s}R^s\otimes_{R^s}R$ and
$R\otimes_{R^s}\alpha R^s\otimes_{R^s}R$ of the middle decomposition, and the two
summands are not isomorphic as *graded* bimodules: they differ by the internal
shift $\{2\}$, so each is the shift of the other, but their graded left ranks
$v^{-1+k}+v^{1+k}$ for $k=-1$ and $k=1$, namely $v^{-2}+v^{0}$ and
$v^{0}+v^{2}$, are different, and an isomorphism of graded bimodules preserves
graded ranks.

Let $1\le i\le n-2$, put $s:=s_i$, $t:=s_{i+1}$ and write
$B_iB_{i+1}B_i:=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i$. Then there are degree-zero
isomorphisms of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_i,\qquad B_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_{i+1},$$
with no additional grading shift on any summand, where $B_{i,i+1,i}$ is the
rank-two longest bimodule of
[[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]]. On split Grothendieck
classes the two decompositions read $[B_iB_{i+1}B_i]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_i]$ and
$[B_{i+1}B_iB_{i+1}]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_{i+1}]$.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] Let $X_0=\{w:\ell(w)\le2\}$. By [F6] the statements $\mathrm S(w)$, $\mathrm hL(w)$, $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold for all $w\in X_0$, and the parameterized ascent statements $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ hold for all $\zeta\ge0$ for the pairs $z<zt$ with $\ell(zt)\le2$; the descent statements of (2) for $X_0$ are the pairs $(z,t)$ with $\ell(z)=2$, $zt<z$, and hold for all $\zeta>0$ by the positive-parameter descent case of [F3] together with the deformation principle [F4] applied on $(0,\infty)$; hence (1) and (2) hold for $X_0$.

**Induction hypothesis and the minimal element.** [ih] Fix a Bruhat ideal $X$ containing $X_0$ for which (1) and (2) hold and assume that every element of $X$ satisfies $\mathrm S$, $\mathrm hL$ and $\mathrm{HR}$; choose $x'$ minimal in the complement of $X$ and write $x'=xs$ with $x\in X$ and $s$ simple. Every $y<x'$ lies in $X$, so $\mathrm S(y)$, $\mathrm hL(y)$, $\mathrm{HR}(y)$ hold for all $y<x'$.

**The lower ascent hypotheses.** Let $t$ be any simple reflection and let $y<x't$ with $y<x'$ and $yt>y$. Then $yt$ is comparable with $x'$: since $\ell(yt)=\ell(y)+1\le\ell(x't)=\ell(x')+1$ and $y<x'$, if $yt\ge x't$ then $\ell(yt)\le\ell(x't)$ forces $yt=x't$, which would give $y=x'$, a contradiction; hence $yt<x'$, so $yt\in X$, and (1) for $X$ applies to the pair $(y,t)$ and gives $\mathrm{HR}(y,t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta\ge0$.

**The lower descent hypotheses.** Let $t$ be simple and $y<x't$ with $y<x'$ and $yt<y$. Then $y\in X$; since $y$ satisfies $\mathrm S(y)$ and $\mathrm hL(y)$, the positive-parameter descent case of [F3] gives $\mathrm hL(y,t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta>0$, and $\mathrm{HR}(y)$ together with [F4] gives $\mathrm{HR}(y,t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta>0$. Hence for every simple $t$ the strong lower hypothesis $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x't,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta>0$.

**Hard Lefschetz for every new ascent pair.** Let $t$ be a simple right descent of $x'$, i.e. $x't<x'$; then $z:=x't\in X$, and we apply the three-case theorem [F3] to the pair $(z,t)$ with $zt=x'$: case (2) with $\zeta>0$ uses $\mathrm S(\le z)$, the lower ascent statements for $z$ (from (1) for $X$) and $\mathrm{HRbar}(<z,t)_\zeta$ (from steps 3.1 and 3.2), and gives $\mathrm hL(z,t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta>0$; case (3) with $\zeta=0$ uses the same lower ascent statements, $\mathrm{HR}(z)$ and $\mathrm hL(w)$ for all $w<zt=x'$ (available since all such $w$ lie in $X$) and gives $\mathrm hL(z,t)_0$. Hence $\mathrm hL(x't,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$ for every right descent $t$ of $x'$.

**Hodge-Riemann for every new ascent pair.** Fix a right descent $t$ of $x'$ and keep $z=x't\in X$. By $\mathrm{HR}(z)$ and the deformation principle [F4] applied on $[0,\infty)$ to the family $\mathrm hL(z,t)_\zeta$, obtained in step 4.1 for all $\zeta\ge0$, the relations $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ hold for all $\zeta\ge0$. In particular the condition (1) holds for $X\cup\{x'\}$: the only new pairs are those with $zt=x'$, i.e. $z=x't$ for the right descents $t$ of $x'$, and these have been verified for all $\zeta\ge0$; all other pairs lie in $X$ and are covered by (1) for $X$.

**Soergel's conjecture for $x'$.** Take the chosen right descent $s$ with $x'=xs$, $x\in X$, and the instance $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$ of step 5.1. Since $\mathrm S(y)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(y)$ hold for all $y<x'$, the embedding theorem [F2] gives that the local intersection forms on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,B_xB_s)$, $y<x'$, are definite for the sign $\mathrm S^\pm(y,x,s)$ and hence non-degenerate; the detection theorem [F1] then gives $\mathrm S(x')$.

**Hard Lefschetz and Hodge-Riemann for $x'$.** By [F5] applied to the pair $(x,s)$ with $\mathrm hL(x,s)_0$ from step 4.1 we obtain $\mathrm hL(x')$; and by [F5] applied to $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ from step 5.1, the restriction of the intersection form to the top summand $B_{x'}$ satisfies HR, which by the now established $\mathrm S(x')$ and the positivity of the comparison scalar [F7] is $\mathrm{HR}(x')$.

**The descent condition for the enlarged ideal.** Let $t$ be simple with $x't<x'$. By step 4.1 we have $\mathrm hL(x',t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta>0$, and $\mathrm{HR}(x')$ from step 7.1, so the deformation principle [F4] applied on the interval $(0,\infty)$ gives $\mathrm{HR}(x',t)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta>0$ (any requested positive parameter is joined to a sufficiently large one by a compact subinterval avoiding $0$). The pairs with $z\in X$ and $zt<z$ are covered by (2) for $X$; hence (2) holds for $X\cup\{x'\}$. Together with step 5.1 this shows that (1) and (2) are preserved by the induction step, and with steps 6.1 and 7.1 that $\mathrm S$, $\mathrm hL$, $\mathrm{HR}$ hold on $X\cup\{x'\}$.

**Conclusion.** The finite induction starting from $X_0$ reaches $X=S_n$, so $\mathrm S(w)$, $\mathrm hL(w)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold for every $w\in S_n$; and for every pair $x,s$ with $xs>x$ the sequence of steps 4.1, 5.1 applied to $z=x$ gives $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ for all $\zeta\ge0$, hence also the strong embedded forms $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ by the positivity of the comparison scalars [F7]. No step restricts a positive middle-position operator to a summand: every passage from the tensor product to its top summand uses the zero-parameter instance and the undeformed restriction lemma [F5], and the positive parameters are handled by the deformation principle on intervals that avoid the singular value $\zeta=0$ in the descent case.

boundaries.reason: The statement requires the finite Bruhat ideal to contain the fixed nonempty initial ideal of elements of length at most two, and the induction of step 2.1 always inspects a proper lower element; no empty ideal or empty lower set arises.

boundaries.evidence: The zero parameter is kept strictly off the descent intervals: step 8.1 applies deformation only on the positive half-line for descents, while the value zero is obtained through the undeformed restriction lemma in step 7.1, so the singular parameter is never approached by a positive interval.
The induction adjoins a single minimal element at a time: step 2.1 chooses one element outside the ideal, and steps 4.1 and 5.1 verify the new ascent pairs one right descent at a time.

The degenerate rank-one and rank-two computations are the base of the induction, handled separately in step 1.1 by direct inspection; no other degenerate configuration (repeated letters, equal parameters) is needed because the induction works on Bruhat ideals.

The two ends of the Bruhat order are the skeleton of the proof: step 1.1 anchors the bottom, and step 9.1 iterates until the top, so the extreme elements of the group are covered by the same induction.
Choice-free: the induction of step 2.1 selects a minimal element of a finite set, and every other construction is a finite verification of the parameterized hypotheses.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is an induction producing three properties for every element of the ideal; none of its clauses is phrased as one direction of an equivalence.
No reverse direction is claimed: the parameterized HR conditions are hypotheses, not conclusions to be characterized.

citations.quote:
Let $X\subseteq S_n$ be a finite Bruhat ideal containing the initial ideal $X_0=\{w:\ell(w)\le2\}$ and assume:

(1) $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$, all $z<zt$ with $zt\in X$ and all simple $t$;

(2) $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta>0$, all $zt<z$ with $z\in X$ and all simple $t$.

Then for every $x\in X$ the three statements $\mathrm S(x)$, $\mathrm hL(x)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ hold. Since (1) and (2) hold for the initial ideal $X_0=\{w:\ell(w)\le2\}$ by direct inspection of the rank-one and rank-two cases, and the induction step below preserves them when passing from an ideal $X$ to $X\cup\{x'\}$ with $x'$ minimal outside $X$, the theorem gives: for every $w\in S_n$, Soergel's conjecture $\mathrm S(w)$, hard Lefschetz $\mathrm hL(w)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold; and for every $x,s$ with $xs>x$ the strong forms $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ hold for all $\zeta\ge0$. The induction below is finite (it runs over the finitely many elements of $S_n$) and uses no choice.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]],
[[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) and let $H_{S_n}$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$ with $q=v^{-2}$ and normalized generators
$H_i=v(T_i+1)$
([[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]). Then there is an
isomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
$$\Phi:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad \Phi([B_i])=H_i=v(T_i+1)\quad(1\le i\le n-1),\qquad \Phi(vX)=v\,\Phi(X),$$
equivalently $\Phi^{-1}(T_i)=v^{-1}[B_i]-1$ for every simple reflection. In
particular the classes satisfy
$$[B_i]^2=(v+v^{-1})[B_i]\qquad\text{in }K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
in agreement with the quadratic relation $H_i^2=(v+v^{-1})H_i$ of the Hecke
algebra, and $\Phi$ is the unique algebra isomorphism with $\Phi([B_i])=H_i$
and $\Phi(v)=v$, because the classes of the $B_i$ together with $v^{\pm1}$
generate $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ as a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

1. $h_\Delta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and
   semilinear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ of the coefficients:
   $h_\nabla(vX)=v^{-1}h_\nabla(X)$ and $h_\nabla([B_i])=H_i$; equivalently
   $h_\nabla=d\circ h_\Delta$, where $d$ is the semilinear algebra involution
   of $H_{S_n}$ determined by $d(v)=v^{-1}$ and $d(T_i)=T_i^{-1}$;
3. for every Bott–Samelson word $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ one has
   $h_\Delta(B_{\underline i})=h_\nabla(B_{\underline i})=H_{i_1}\cdots H_{i_r}$,
   and for every bimodule $M$ in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$ and simple reflection
   $s_i$ the simple-generator recursion
   $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$,
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$ holds; in the Elias–Williamson
   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

Let $M=B_x^R$ over $S$ and let $s$ be a right descent, $xs<x$. Assume $\mathrm{S}(x)$. Then there is a graded $(S,S^s)$-bimodule $N$ and an isomorphism $M\cong N\otimes_{S^s}S$. Consequently $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$; choosing the decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ in the middle tensor factor, the reduced operator $L_\zeta$ has, with respect to the resulting identification $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, the matrix
$$L_\zeta=\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix},$$
where the scalar off-diagonal entry is a degree-two map $M(1)\to M(-1)$. The construction requires no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$. If $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ also holds and $\zeta>0$, this matrix satisfies centered hard Lefschetz; at $\zeta=0$ it fails centered hard Lefschetz.

The hard Lefschetz theorem for $L_\zeta$ on $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ holds in the following three cases.

(1) $\zeta>0$ and $xs<x$: under $\mathrm S(x)$, $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ implies $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$. The $\mathrm{hL}(x)$-only descent implication, with the same matrix and without an assumed $\mathrm S(x)$, is retained as an after-induction consequence in the character theorem, where $\mathrm S(x)$ has already been proved.

(2) $\zeta>0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds.

(3) $\zeta=0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(z)$ for all $z<xs$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$ holds.

In the remaining case $\zeta=0$ and $xs<x$, centered hard Lefschetz fails: in the decomposition $B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ the operator $L_0$ is diagonal, the bottom vector of the first summand lies in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and its $(\ell(x)+1)$-st $\rho$-power is zero, while the opposite total degree is nonzero by self-duality; the two copies have Lefschetz strings centered at $-1$ and $+1$ rather than at zero.

derivations.claim: **Soergel's conjecture for all elements.** The simultaneous induction theorem [F1] applies with $X=S_n$: its two parameterized HR conditions are verified for every Bruhat ideal along the induction, and its conclusion gives $\mathrm S(w)$, $\mathrm hL(w)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ for every $w\in S_n$. By the definition of $\mathrm S(w)$ this is $\operatorname{ch}(B_w^R)=\underline H_w$ for every $w$, which is the character statement; the same theorem also gives the strong embedded forms $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for all $x,s$ with $xs>x$ and all $\zeta\ge0$.

**The class and the rational form.** By [F2], $\operatorname{ch}(M)=\Phi([M])$ for the split-Grothendieck isomorphism $\Phi:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}\to H$, with $\Phi([B_s])=H_s+v$ in the normalized standard basis. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(B_w^R)=\underline H_w$ from step 1.1 means precisely $\Phi([B_w^R])=\underline H_w$. Real scalar extension preserves indecomposable labels, shifts and support-filtration multiplicities, so its character agrees with the rational character in the same integral Hecke algebra. The equality proved over $\mathbb R$ therefore gives the same character equality over $\mathbb Q$, and the rational $B_w$ categorifies the same Kazhdan--Lusztig basis element. No inverse map from $H$ to $K_0$ is used as an object character.

**Hodge-theoretic statements.** The hard Lefschetz property $\mathrm hL(w)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ for all $w$ are part of the conclusion of the simultaneous induction in step 1.1; the signs are the standard signs of the dictionary, normalized by the positive bottom Lefschetz form.

**The unconditional descent consequence.** Let $xs<x$ be a right descent. Since $\mathrm S(x)$ now holds for every $x$, the descent lemma [F3] displays the matrix of $L_\zeta$ on $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$; combining it with $\mathrm hL(x)$ from step 2.2 and $\zeta>0$ gives $\mathrm hL(x,s)_\zeta$, with no character hypothesis beyond the already established $\mathrm S(x)$, and the same lemma records the failure of centered hard Lefschetz at $\zeta=0$ through the vanishing $(\ell(x)+1)$-st power of $\rho$ on the bottom class of $B_x(1)$ while the opposite total degree is nonzero by self-duality.

**Conclusion.** Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give the character statement in the real and rational categories, step 2.2 the Hodge-theoretic statements with the standard signs, and step 3.1 the unconditional descent consequence; no step assumes positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials, which is instead a corollary of the character identity, and no step uses a result beyond the suppliers listed. This proves the theorem.

boundaries.reason: The theorem quantifies over the finite symmetric group and its fixed indecomposable bimodules; there is no family construction or empty aggregate in its claims.

boundaries.evidence: Current step 3.1 cites [F3] for the descent matrix and records centered hard Lefschetz failure at zeta=0; step 2.1 fixes ch=Phi and Phi([B_s])=standard H_s+v. This references the already sealed numbered clauses only.

The unit label and the unit class are the normalization anchors: the trivial element has unit character, and the generator normalization of the Grothendieck isomorphism is used in step 2.1 to compare the class statement with the character identity.

No genericity in the Hecke parameter is used: step 1.1 applies the simultaneous induction over the finite Bruhat order, and the only singular parameter value, the zero deformation, is handled separately in step 3.1.

The extreme elements of the group are covered by the same induction: step 2.2 records that the Hodge-theoretic statements for every element are part of the conclusion of step 1.1, so the bottom and top elements are not exceptions.
Choice-free: the induction underlying step 1.1 runs over the finite set of permutations, and the descent computation of step 3.1 is a finite matrix identity.
Current step 2.1 uses ch(M)=Phi([M]), with Phi:K0_split→H and Phi([B_s])=H_s+v in the normalized standard basis; the character and class statements are the same equality under this map.
The same current step 2.1 identification ch(M)=Phi([M]) reads the class equality back as the object-character equality; the map is not described as its inverse.

citations.quote: For every $w\in S_n$ the character of the indecomposable type-$A$ Soergel bimodule equals the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element: $\operatorname{ch}(B_w^R)=\underline H_w$. Equivalently, the class $[B_w^R]$ in the split Grothendieck group corresponds to $\underline H_w$ under the Hecke algebra isomorphism, and the extension of scalars of the rational $B_w$ categorifies the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis. Moreover the hard Lefschetz property $\mathrm hL(w)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold for every $w$, with the standard signs, and the same identities hold for the rational category by the base-change comparison. Finally, for every right descent $xs<x$ the matrix of $L_\zeta$ on $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix}$; for $\zeta>0$, $\mathrm hL(x)$ implies $\mathrm hL(x,s)_\zeta$ without any additional character hypothesis, since $\mathrm S$ is now established for all elements, while at $\zeta=0$ centered hard Lefschetz fails.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

1. $h_\Delta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and
   semilinear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ of the coefficients:
   $h_\nabla(vX)=v^{-1}h_\nabla(X)$ and $h_\nabla([B_i])=H_i$; equivalently
   $h_\nabla=d\circ h_\Delta$, where $d$ is the semilinear algebra involution
   of $H_{S_n}$ determined by $d(v)=v^{-1}$ and $d(T_i)=T_i^{-1}$;
3. for every Bott–Samelson word $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ one has
   $h_\Delta(B_{\underline i})=h_\nabla(B_{\underline i})=H_{i_1}\cdots H_{i_r}$,
   and for every bimodule $M$ in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$ and simple reflection
   $s_i$ the simple-generator recursion
   $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$,
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$ holds; in the Elias–Williamson
   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]],
[[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) and let $H_{S_n}$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$ with $q=v^{-2}$ and normalized generators
$H_i=v(T_i+1)$
([[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]). Then there is an
isomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
$$\Phi:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad \Phi([B_i])=H_i=v(T_i+1)\quad(1\le i\le n-1),\qquad \Phi(vX)=v\,\Phi(X),$$
equivalently $\Phi^{-1}(T_i)=v^{-1}[B_i]-1$ for every simple reflection. In
particular the classes satisfy
$$[B_i]^2=(v+v^{-1})[B_i]\qquad\text{in }K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
in agreement with the quadratic relation $H_i^2=(v+v^{-1})H_i$ of the Hecke
algebra, and $\Phi$ is the unique algebra isomorphism with $\Phi([B_i])=H_i$
and $\Phi(v)=v$, because the classes of the $B_i$ together with $v^{\pm1}$
generate $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ as a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

derivations.claim: **The coefficients in the standard basis (1).** By [F1] we have $\operatorname{ch}(B_w^R)=\underline H_w$; expanding both sides in the standard basis, the left side has coefficients given by the $\Delta$-multiplicities, which are nonnegative integers by [F2], and the right side has coefficients $h_{y,w}$ by definition. Hence $h_{y,w}=\sum_d(B_w:\Delta_y(d))v^d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v]$. Passing to the classical normalization $P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-(\ell(w)-\ell(y))}h_{y,w}$ of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial displays its coefficients as the same nonnegative multiplicities and therefore nonnegative integers; in particular the $\mu$-coefficient, the coefficient of $v$ in $h_{y,w}$, is a sum of multiplicities and hence nonnegative. This proves (1).

**The structure constants (2).** The tensor product decomposes into finitely many normalized indecomposables with graded multiplicities, $B_x^RB_y^R=\bigoplus_zB_z^R(m_z)$ with $m_z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v^{\pm1}]$. Applying the class map $\Phi$ of [F3] and using multiplicativity, $\underline H_x\underline H_y=\Phi([B_x^RB_y^R])=\sum_zm_z\underline H_z$, so that $\mu^z_{x,y}=m_z$; the multiplicity space of $B_z^R$ in the tensor product has character $m_z$ by definition of the multiplicity, which proves (2).

**The standard-basis product (3).** By [F2] the character of the tensor product $B_xB_y$ is a nonnegative integer combination of standard basis elements, $\operatorname{ch}(B_xB_y)=\sum_{y',d}(B_xB_y:\Delta_{y'}(d))v^dH_{y'}$, and by multiplicativity of the character and [F1] it equals the product $\operatorname{ch}(B_x)\operatorname{ch}(B_y)=\underline H_x\underline H_y$. Comparing coefficients gives that the expansion of the product in the standard basis has exactly the $\Delta$-multiplicities as coefficients, and these are nonnegative integers. This proves (3) and completes the corollary.

boundaries.evidence: The sums over the Bruhat interval and over the decomposition labels are finite and nonempty because the coefficient of the top basis element in its own expansion is one; steps 1.1 and 2.1 expand them explicitly and no empty sum is given a special value.

Vanishing coefficients are permitted and classified: step 1.1 produces nonnegative integer combinations whose coefficients may be zero, and step 2.1 allows a structure constant to vanish when the corresponding summand is absent.

The leading coefficient is one: the top coefficient of the Kazhdan-Lusztig element is one in the triangularity input of step 1.1, and the unit label contributes the coefficient one to the product expansion of step 2.1.

The degenerate case of equal factors in the product is included: step 2.1 derives nonnegativity of the structure constants without excluding repeated labels, and step 3.1 treats the standard-basis product for arbitrary pairs.

Both ends of each Bruhat interval are read off: step 1.1 controls the coefficient at the bottom and at the top of the interval through the triangular change of basis, and both extremes are nonnegative in the conclusion.
Choice-free: the argument reads off multiplicities of finite standard flags in steps 1.1 and 3.1 and applies the character theorem; no selection from an infinite family is made.

Forward translation of the equivalence in clause (1): the standard-basis nonnegativity obtained in step 1.1 converts into nonnegativity of the classical Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial coefficients through the normalization dictionary of the triangular expansion.

Reverse translation: nonnegative polynomial coefficients give nonnegative standard-basis coefficients by the same invertible triangular change of basis used in step 1.1, so the two formulations of positivity are equivalent.

citations.quote:
**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad
   \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad
   \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Equivalently, $w\rho$ is positive on $\alpha_i^\vee$ exactly when $s_iw$ is
longer than $w$, so the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The bottom degree of $B_x^R$ is $-\ell(x)$ and its
top degree is $+\ell(x)$; on a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
